en: The *Nyāyamukha-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Introduction to Logic), composed by Dharma Master Tai.

Regarding the initial statement "Nyāya" (*Inming*): among the five branches of knowledge (*pañcavidyā*), it refers to the treatises on logic; that is, it is the general name for all treatises on Nyāya.
The *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Gate of Right Reasoning) is an alternative title for this treatise. Regarding the term "reason" (*hetu*) mentioned at the outset, there are two types:

first, the productive cause (*janana-hetu*), and second, the revealing cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*). What is being discussed here primarily elucidates the revealing cause, while also incidentally clarifying the productive cause.
Within the revealing cause, there are further three types; the first is the "reason of meaning" (*artha-hetu*), which refers generally to that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
The meaning of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is the first; the statement [of that] is the second, the reason of words (śabda-hetu);

and the cognition [of it] is the third, the reason of knowledge (jñāna-hetu). For all opponents as well as those who establish the thesis, the mental states and mental factors that understand the aforementioned reasons of meaning and words are collectively termed "knowledge.
These three reasons together are able to illuminate the impermanence of sound, just like a lamp.
It illuminates objects; therefore, it is called "illumination" (*prakāśa*). This is a designation based on its object: "illumination" is a synonym for wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, this very wisdom of illumination can illuminate its causal objects and thoroughly realize the fundamental principle; thus, it is called "Hetuvidyā" (Logic/Etymology).

In this case, the phrase "the cause is itself the illumination" constitutes the verbal expression, and it is named *Hetuvidyā*. First, because it arises from the cause of illumination, its name is derived from that cause.
"Clear. Second, it is called *hetuvidyā* (Logic) because it is the cause for clarity; thus, it is named *hetuvidyā* from the perspective of its result.

Alternatively, if "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the object of knowledge, it is named *hetuvidyā*. Another explanation is that "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the aforementioned complete range of objects of wisdom, while "clarity" (*vidyā*) means "discernment.
This treatise discerns and clarifies these causes, and is therefore named *hetuvidyā*. These two characters, *hetuvidyā*, follow this [etymological] principle.
The *Pramāṇa-śāstra* states that "object" (*artha*) is a name. Regarding the term "correct principle" (*yukti*): wisdom (*buddhi*) illuminates the principle;

it is named from the cause of the principle for speech. Since the principle gives rise to speech, speech is also called a principle. That which is illuminated as the object of wisdom is likewise called a principle.

Among principles, there are those that are correct and those that are erroneous; to exclude the erroneous, one says "correct. This "correct principle" (*samyag-yukti*) is the gateway through which this treatise functions, enabling one to attain realization and understanding. Therefore...
It is called the *Nyāyamukha* (The Gateway to Reasoning). Furthermore, another interpretation is that "Reasoning" (*nyāya*) refers to the fifty-odd treatises such as the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*;
since this treatise serves as a gateway to them, it is named *Nyāyamukha*. Regarding the title *Nyāyapraveśa* (Introduction to Reasoning) composed by the Lord of Devas (Dignāga):

this treatise is named "Reasoning," and because one can enter into it [through this work], it is called *Nyāyapraveśa*. The word "gateway" (*mukha*) is omitted for brevity; it is just like [the term] "ascending."

The "Gate of the Stages" (*nyāyamukha*) is a title established by the Lord of Devas (*Devendra*). Furthermore, it is like entering a room by way of a door; as this treatise states, it is called a "gate" (*mukha*).
Another interpretation is that "Right Reasoning" (*nyāya*) refers to the principles of phenomena (*dharmadharmatā*). Is there such a thing as right or wrong?
Now, taking this treatise as the gate, one attains correct wisdom and awakens to the ultimate Right Reasoning; therefore, it is named the "Gate of Right Reasoning. It says:
As for "Right Reasoning" (*nyāya*), it refers to works such as the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga, which elucidate the correct principles of all phenomena.
This treatise serves as a gateway for entering into those works.
As for the "Great Domain Dragon" (Mahāviṣaya-nāga): its original pronunciation is Mahā-viṣaya-nāga. *Mahā* means "great"; *viṣaya* means "domain";
and *nāga* means "dragon. This bodhisattva is so named because he possesses great majestic power (*mahā-tejas*), like a dragon of a vast domain.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of desire" and so forth:
this treatise, as a single work, is divided into three parts. This first section is the introductory and prolegomenal part (*nidāna-bhāga*).

The second part, beginning from the words "the various expressions of the primary doctrine" (*mūla-artha*), is the main body of the exposition (*siddhānta-bhāga*). The third part consists of the four lines at the end of the treatise, which reveal...

This is the section for conforming to reality. Since antiquity, the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) and the various Great and Small Vehicles (*yāna*) have each established their own systems of logic (*hetuvidyā*), presenting both proof and refutation.
Now, within these systems of proof and refutation, I wish to distinguish the brilliance of wisdom from mere words, thereby grasping the truth.

This refers to the "Wisdom-Logic" (*jñāna-hetuvidyā*): it is the discernment of what is not a fallacy as a fallacy, and what is a fallacy as not being a fallacy; herein, I shall now manifest this discrimination.
The wise understand that this [fallacious] proof and refutation is indeed a fault; it is not the case that what is not a fault is called "not a fault.

This means that both the semblance of a proof (*sādhana*) and the semblance of a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) are termed "proof" and "refutation" respectively. The actual meaning of "proof" and "refutation" refers to the genuine proof and refutation; one does not exclusively grasp the faultless proof and refutation as such.
The thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth; one phrase is as in other places.
Among these, [the phrase] up to "is called the thesis" constitutes the thesis.

There are four kinds. First, a position commonly accepted by all, such as saying "the blue lotus has fragrance"; this is not established because it falls into the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Second, a position derived from one's own tradition; this is also not established because it falls into the fallacy of proving what is already established within that very teaching.

Third, a position consisting solely of the meaning (*artha-mātra-pakṣa*), such as establishing that sound is impermanent, or that [the self] is merely empty and without self (*śūnyatā-anātman*); it is not...

Because it does not establish what it itself posits, there is no fault. This is the fourth [type], the *svābhiprāyika* (proposition according to one’s own intention), which even within its own teaching establishes the tenets of other teachings. For details, see other sources.

Regarding the statement that "it is not the case that those characteristics are [merely] dispelled," there are five fallacies in the thesis (*pakṣa*). These are termed "contradiction of the meaning" (*arthaviruddha*), because these five fallacies constitute a contradiction between the meaning and the thesis.
This is the meaning of contradiction. That which can dispel [the opponent's view] and lead to the synthesis of the ultimate point is called the "ultimate thesis" (*siddhānta*).
As for the realization of the meaning through the thesis: it is that which leads to the ultimate.
This is similar to the explanation of the *Kṣudraka-viśeṣa*. Therefore, regarding the "establisher" (*sādhana*),
[the author] cites various treatises composed by Vasubandhu, which also establish that a single reason (*hetu*) or two reasons— when expressed as multiple words— are called the "establisher."
This serves as proof for the preceding text concerning the *Vādanyāya* and other such works; "and so forth" (*ādi*) here includes the *Vādavidhi* and the *Vādahṛdaya*.

These three treatises were all composed by Vasubandhu. Furthermore, regarding other treatises on inference (*anumāna*) such as the *Vādanyāya*, they all establish their proofs (*sādhana*) through one reason (*hetu*) and two examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Regarding the phrase "from one statement" up to "establishing the nature":

among the three statements beginning with the "thesis" (pakṣa) in the verse, these are collectively termed the "prover" (sādhana). This is to clarify the single reason (hetu) and the two examples (dṛṣṭānta).
They collectively constitute a single nature as a probans (*sādhana*), just as many things—such as rafters, beams, walls, and doors—collectively constitute a single house.
One cannot argue that because the rafters and other components are multiple, the house must also be multiple.
Regarding the phrase "from this [point] up to establishing the fault":

among the three members—thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—the absence of any one of them is called a "deficiency" (*nyūna*), which constitutes a fault in the nature of the proof (*sādhana*).
Prior to Dignāga, if it was said that the thesis was missing, or that the reason or example was missing, it was termed a fault in the proof. One master explains: "Self..."
There are three cases where there is a thesis but no reason or example; one case where there is a reason but no thesis or example; and one case where there is an example but no thesis or reason.
There is a case where there is a thesis and a reason but no example; a case where there is a thesis and an example but no reason; and a case where there is a reason and an example but no thesis.
With the reason and example as the seventh case, these seven cases are termed "deficiencies in the nature of the proof" (*sādhana-nyūnatā-doṣa*).
Furthermore, another master explains: "The previous [cases] regarding the 'phrases' may be so; however, the seventh case cannot be. If one or two minor elements remain, one may say it is deficient;
but in the seventh, since neither the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), nor the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) exist, how can it be called deficient?"

Therefore, this is not permissible. Dignāga stated that there is the fault of deficiency (*ūnatva*) within the probans (*hetu*) when it exists in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) but not in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
Bhadanta Śrīlāta previously explained the master’s [Dignāga’s] words as follows: there are cases where the probans exists, yet neither a similar nor a dissimilar instance exists.

There are cases where there is a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) but no reason (*hetu*) and no dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*); cases where there is a dissimilar instance but no reason and no similar instance; and cases where both are missing, which constitute three propositions.
Furthermore, there are cases where there is a reason and a similar instance but no dissimilar instance; cases where there is a similar and a dissimilar instance but no reason;

and cases where there is a dissimilar instance and a reason that is itself the similar instance; these, with one element missing, constitute three propositions. Finally, there are cases where there is neither a reason nor either a similar or a dissimilar instance. These constitute...
Regarding the seventh alternative: after the Master [Dharmakīrti] has already established the reality [of the probans], he does not posit a seventh alternative, as has been explained previously.
As for the statement that this constitutes a fault in the proof (sādhana), this is merely an interpretation of the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "In this [context]... [up to] ...is called" (*asmin... ity ucyate*):
the commentary explains that this marks the beginning of a topical section (*śākhā-vākya*).

Just as in this region one uses terms such as "now," "if," or "as for" to introduce a new section, this serves to explain the meaning of the first proposition (*pakṣa*) of the preceding [verse]. Therefore, it says "in this. Next, the commentary explains: "This is the thesis (*pakṣa*), etc."
Within the midst of many words, one excludes the examples of the soil and the cause, retaining only the thesis (*pakṣa*). Therefore, each is "the midst.

This means that by raising up the hands (the arch) to grasp the specific, it is said to be "the midst" within the thesis and so forth; thus it is called "the midst. Alternatively, "excluding and retaining" means excluding the extremes of exaggeration and depreciation while retaining what is grasped as the middle.
That is to say, calling fallacious theses, reasons, or examples true is called "exaggeration" (*samāropa*); whereas [calling] true theses, reasons...
"Metaphor" (*dṛṣṭānta*) refers to that which is not true; it is termed "damage" (*hāni*). This excludes these two extremes and upholds the Middle Way.

This is precisely what was meant above by the "true meaning" within the context of establishing and refuting arguments. Question: If true speech is called "damage" when it is not true, why is similar speech not so designated when it is not similar?
Answer: "True" refers to the correct principle for delivering sentient beings; when this is not true, it is given the name "damage."
It might be argued that what appears to be [the thesis] but is not actually so constitutes a fallacy (*hāni*), yet this is irrational and is not termed a "reduction" (*nyūna*).

Furthermore, it may also be subsumed under the treatise itself. Question: Since this passage explains the true thesis (*siddhānta*), why is it that within this context, the "similar" (*pratibimba*) is also considered the "middle" (*madhya*)?

Answer: The fourth line of the verse states: "That which is contrary to it cannot dispel [the fault]. This specifically excludes the "similar" thesis. One should know that the first three lines constitute the framework (*paddhati*).

This includes both the general terminology and the true and the similar. Furthermore, it is explained that the word "among" (*madhye*) refers specifically to within the True School (*satya-samaya*) and so forth;
this is how it is known. Since the verse states that what is to be established is called the "thesis" (*pakṣa*), it cannot be refuted by a meaning that contradicts it.
One should understand that the thesis (pakṣa) stated in the preceding sentence cannot be refuted by a meaning contrary to it.

If one were to say that the preceding sentence also applies to a pseudo-thesis (pratipakṣa), then the subsequent sentence should likewise apply to both the genuine and the pseudo. Regarding the phrase "among these, such as the thesis":
Its three components—the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—are all free from the two extremes of superimposition and denial.

That is to say, by avoiding the extremes of superimposition and denial within that [middle], it adopts the Middle Way; therefore, it is called "the middle" (*madhya*). Alternatively, it may be understood as distinguishing this from the three categories of the heterodox, the provisional, and the orthodox; hence it is called "the middle."
Regarding the phrase "only taking [the thesis]," etc.:

this intends to distinguish the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) so as to specifically take up the thesis (*pakṣa*). Alternatively, it may mean that one can exclude the reason and the example to specifically select the thesis;

this is what is meant by the sense of "discrimination" (*pariccheda*). If one were merely re-explaining the meaning of "selective retention" from the previous [passage], one would likewise have to say "specifically taking" (*parigraha*), rather than "specifically selecting."
"Only" (*kevala*) means to exclude. Second, "excludable" (*vivecanīya*) refers to discernment (*vivecana*). Discernment consists of selecting what is correct and excluding what is incorrect.

That is to say, if it is the thesis (*pakṣa*), it is selected; if it is the probans (*sādhana*), it is excluded. "Distinct" (*bhinna*) has the sense of difference, and it also applies to both exclusion and inclusion.

That is, one excludes the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) as distinct, while taking the thesis as distinct. If that is so, since the word "exclude" (*vivecana*) is already sufficient, why is it necessary [to add "only"]?

"Distinct. Answer: "Distinguishing" (*jian*) is a general term; here, "distinguishing away" (*jianqu*) refers to specific differentiation (*vibhāga*), not to "distinguishing and retaining" (*jianchi*) and so forth.

Therefore, it is further specified as "distinct. Regarding the phrase "established according to one's own intention": [this refers to the fact that] the names are established according to the individual's own perspective.
There are four types of tenets, as explained previously. The fourth is the tenet established according to one's own inclination (*yathābhiprāya*).

This is exemplified by Sāṃmitīyas who, having already demonstrated their eloquence, disregard the tenets of the three preceding treatises; within their own school, they follow their own intentions and provisionally assume the role of other teachers to establish other doctrinal positions.
This is called "establishing according to one's own intention," and thus it is without fault.
Regarding the phrase "desiring to establish" (*iṣṭa-sādhya*) up to "named as the thesis" (*pakṣa-nāman*):
the two characters "action" (*karma*) exclude [the fallacies of] similar reasons and examples; the two characters "that which is established" (*sādhya*) exclude true reasons and examples.
To say "desiring to establish that which is to be proven" means that all proponents merely intend in their minds to make something the object of proof; the proponent merely intends...
The thesis (*pakṣa*) established by the activity of proof is what one wishes to establish; therefore, it is called "that which is intended to be established" (*sādhya*).

This is the fundamental intention of the proponent (*vādī*). Since the true reason (*hetu*) and the true example (*dṛṣṭānta*) have already been previously validated, they are not intended to be the means of proof (*sādhana*).
If this term "intended to be" were omitted and one simply said that "the established is the thesis," it would fail to distinguish [the thesis] from the true [reason and example].

Regarding the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*): that which possesses the nature of being capable of establishing [the thesis] is called the "probandum" (*sādhya*). As for pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and pseudo-examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), they must further be established;

thus, they should also be considered theses (*pakṣa*). However, although they are indeed probanda, they are not what the proponent originally intends to establish. Although they are probanda, they are not theses.
Regarding the statement that pseudo-reasons must further be established, there are two types of grammatical treatises (*śabdavidyā-śāstra*).
There are two positions: first, that sound arises from conditions and is not extinguished; second, that sound is merely manifested by conditions and is neither produced nor extinguished.

For example, when a follower of the Buddha debates with a proponent of the *śabdabrahma* (phonetic monism) doctrine, he establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*) that "sound is impermanent" because it is "something produced," using "an atom" as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Against this proponent of the manifestation theory of sound, this reason (*hetu*) commits the fallacy of "non-establishment of at least one of the two [probandum or probans]."
[This is] a fallacy (*sādhana-vaikalya*). Because that opposing debater does not admit that sound is a product (*kṛtaka*), the reason must be further established.
[The proof is: "Sound is a product because it is maintained as a real entity by conditions" (the reason), "just like a jar, etc. (the similar instance).
Furthermore, regarding the example of atoms (*paramāṇu*), because the opposing debater does not admit them to be impermanent, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
[Response: This is a fault. However, it must further be established as follows: "The atom (paramāṇu) is impermanent" (the thesis); "because it possesses material obstruction" (the reason);
"just like a jar and so forth" (the similar example). The Śabdika school posits that the atom is permanent;

yet, because it is resistant (sapratigha), this reason and example, when accepted as established, are indeed what is to be proven (sādhya). Nevertheless, the intention of the proponent at that time was only...
One delights in the thesis (*pakṣa*) as that which is to be established. One does not delight in establishing fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) or fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).

Furthermore, it is explained: one delights in the thesis as that which is to be established, because the thesis is not [itself] established; rather, it is that which is to be established. That is to say, one does not delight in [fallacious] reasons and examples, nor does one establish what is not a valid reason or example.
If it were otherwise, and one delighted in the thesis as that which is to be established while the activity [of proof] were the means of establishment, [then the fault would follow].

If one were to say that the pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and pseudo-examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*)—which are not established or are re-established—are also of the nature of the means of proof (*sādhanatva*), then they too should be called the thesis (*pakṣa*).

However, although pseudo-reasons and pseudo-examples may be further established, at the time they are attained, they are solely of the nature of the means of proof and are not the thesis to be proven.
Therefore, it is known that what is intended to be proven is the thesis, while that which serves as the means of proof is not intended to be proven.
The thesis is established by means of fallacious reasons and fallacious examples. The establishment of the reason and the example is as previously explained.
This text is precisely that which enters into the principle (*nyāya*) according to one's own preference. However, this text lacks a subject (*dharmin*) that is universally established;

rather, it concerns a property (*dharma*) characterized by a universally established distinction. The Master of the Treatise explains: Śaṅkara does not delight in this treatise, just as [it is] with the Sāṃkhya.

Regarding the debate with the Śākyaputrīyas, the establishment of the vehicle (*yāna*) as a reason is an act of grace. However, it shares the fault of being an unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddha*) within the reason itself.
Since a reason must be established upon a factual locus (*dharmin*), and that factual locus does not exist [for them], the reason is unestablished.

It is precisely because the opponent does not believe in our [position] that they establish the vehicle as having the fault of "cutting off existence" (*bhāvaviccheda*). This is called an "extremely established qualifier" (*prasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), just like [the argument regarding] the Buddha.
The Cowherd repeatedly engaged in debate, establishing that sound has the property of cessation (*nirodha*) and the removal of affliction (*kleśa*).

This [position] inherently suffers from the fallacy of lacking a similar instance (*asādharmya-dṛṣṭānta-nyūna*), because the Sāṃkhya school does not admit the existence of a dharma characterized by the cessation of affliction; thus, no such example exists.

It is precisely because they do not believe that sound possesses the cessation of affliction that [the opponent] establishes the cessation of affliction as a consequence, yet even this is subject to refutation. As for the term "nature of meaning" (*artha-svabhāva*), it is like the thesis statement: "Sound is..."
It is impermanent. Regarding the distinction between the characteristic of impermanence and sound, the ultimate word is that it must necessarily be so.
Why then should one further employ words of distinction to effect a distinction? Therefore, this comparative argument is a statement beyond comparison.
Regarding the statement "in order to manifest [the meaning] up to 'dispelling'":
this refers to the fact that the tenets established by other non-Buddhists and the like involve five kinds of faults.
Now, because one wishes to manifest the avoidance of the faults inherent in the tenets established by those other non-Buddhists, there is the fourth phrase. It may also be established as faulty.
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is a thesis that is free from fault; it is distinct from others. Now, wishing to clarify that which is distinct from other faulty theses, these words are spoken.
Regarding the phrase "it does not negate the meaning of contradiction with that," this is the explicit text, though it is merely abbreviated by lacking the word "able" (*śakya*).
As for the "meaning of contradiction," it refers to the fact that the thesis contradicts the correct thesis, and thus constitutes a contradictory meaning.
This very thesis (*pakṣa*) is not sublated by a pseudo-thesis (*pratipakṣa*); therefore, it is said that its meaning is "non-contradictory" (*aviruddha*).
That which can negate the expressed meaning of words is precisely what constitutes a "contradictory meaning. The term "words" (*śabda*) refers to the meaning (*artha*) conveyed below them.

"Negation" (*apoha*) carries the sense of removal or refutation. This particular point does not exist within the *Nyāyapraveśa*. Although, as previously stated, the action (*karman*) was taken as the probandum (*sādhya*), nevertheless...

The thesis has not yet been established. It must first eliminate five faults before it can become a valid thesis. The following passage [shows] that the contradictions with the meaning cannot be dispelled.
If they are not what is to be dispelled...
The verbal expression that contradicts the meaning refers precisely to the avoidance of the five fallacies. The meaning intended by the words of a true doctrine is contrary to a faulty doctrine;
therefore, it is called "contradictory meaning. If there is a faulty doctrine, it is sublated by its contradictory, faultless, true meaning.
If there is a faultless doctrine, it is sublated by its contradictory, true doctrine. This is precisely what [is meant].
If a thesis is not that which is excluded by the statement of the five faults of a thesis, it is called a "true thesis.

This means that within the context of the mutual substitution of the five faulty theses as the excluders, the true thesis is what is to be excluded. The following passage presents the excluder to demonstrate that this [faulty] excluder cannot exclude the true thesis.
Furthermore, it is explained that when the [faulty] thesis is compared with the true thesis, it is not capable of excluding it.

Because it possesses faults, it is said that this is not what is excluded by the words expressing a meaning contrary to that [true doctrine]. That is to say, the true doctrine has that which is excluded;
the five faults cited below, when compared to the true doctrine, serve solely as that which is excluded, thereby demonstrating that they are not the agents of exclusion.
This is the explanation of the fourth line of the verse.

To establish [a position] up to this point as false is the fallacy of self-contradiction in one's own words. That is to say, there is a non-Buddhist who establishes that all speech is entirely unreal.
This very speech you have uttered contradicts itself. Why? Because when you say that all speech is false, is the speech from your own mouth true or false?
If you say it is true, for what reason do you claim that everything is false speech? If you yourself say it is false, then all other speech must be true.
Furthermore, if you attempt to defend yourself by saying, "Understand the meaning within my mouth..."

Regarding the statement that all other speech is false: suppose there is a second person who, upon hearing what you have said—that all speech is false—immediately speaks in reply, saying, "These words of yours are true. Now, is this person's utterance false or true?
If you say it is false, then your own words are void. If you say it is true, why do you then claim [that all speech is false]?
Setting aside what I have said, suppose one were to offer this defense: "Excluding the path, my words alone are true for this one person;
excluding all those who have attained awakening, they are entirely false. If that were so, a third person might then say: "The words of this second person are also true.
Now, would the words of this third person be false or true? If you say they are false, then this third...
If the words of both of these first persons are true, they ought to be false;
yet if the words of the third person are true, why do you say that, excluding myself and this person, all others are false?

If one first [establishes] that sound is impermanent and later asserts that it is permanent, this contradicts one's own teaching; it is also called a contradiction with one's own tenet (*svasiddhānta-virodha*).

Within the system of the Ulūkyas (Vaiśeṣikas), they first establish that sound is non-eternal, yet then assert that sound is eternal; thus, within their own school, they contradict what was previously established.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because [the reason] exists in common," this contradicts worldly convention.
That is to say, if within the thesis being established, [the reason] is "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa), such as when one claims that the moon is defined solely by its having a hare;
since there is no other similar phenomenon that is the moon, this moon [is unique] relative to others.
The property [of being the moon] does not exist elsewhere; therefore, it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). Furthermore, because its nature is exactly as it has been heard, this reason is unshared.
Since it is an unshared property in common with the subject, there can be no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or the like;

only then is the inference (*anumāna*) established. Thus, it is said that there is no inference. When a fool sees that there is no inference to establish [the moon] as the moon, he then establishes it immediately, saying:
This is not the moon. Although it is established as such [for the proponent], it serves to exclude the meaning that contradicts what is commonly said by the world to be the moon.
The term "universally acknowledged" (*prasiddha*) refers to what the world collectively accepts as the moon. The term "speaker" (*vādin*) refers to the one who utters the word "moon.
The "contradictory meaning" (*viruddhārtha*) is the common, accepted meaning conveyed by the word itself. It is this very common, accepted meaning that is capable of...
The statement that "what has been established [by others] is set aside" does not mean that it is not the sense of being contrary to the moon.

If this is the only interpretation, then the previous statement that "that which is contrary to the thesis is not able to set aside the meaning of its opposite" does not refer to a contradiction with the true thesis or a contradiction with the characteristics of the thesis.
Rather, it means that if a thesis is established and possesses faults, it is then in contradiction with the five kinds of reasoning; it is these reasonings that [are meant].

Because it contradicts the thesis, it is called "contradictory meaning. Since the true thesis accords with reason, it does not share the same status as that pseudo-thesis which is set aside as contradictory meaning;
therefore, it is said that this [true thesis] cannot be set aside by that contradictory meaning. Question:
As in the case of contradicting one's own words, what constitutes the reason? Answer: It is the reason known by the opponent in the debate. This is appropriate.
This constitutes the fault of contradicting one’s own statement; this is the logical principle. To illustrate with a specific case:
it is like asserting the thesis (pakṣa) that "the hare-marked [object] is not the moon," with the reason (hetu) that "it exists," and using "the sun and so forth" as the example (dṛṣṭānta).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also [the claim] that [it is] permanent, etc.," this statement contains two fallacies: namely, contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and contradiction with inference (*anumāna*).
The term "also in the subject" (*dharmi*) refers to the thesis (*pakṣa*). An example of a subject is as when one says "sound" or "pot. That which is established therein is...
This means that the proponent of the thesis establishes upon the subject (*dharmin*) "sound" the property (*dharma*) of being "not audible," or establishes "permanence" with respect to a "jar.
Alternatively, "that very same [proponent]" may establish the meanings of "not audible" and "permanent" upon that very subject;
these are the properties of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*). This is stated for this purpose.

Regarding the refutation of meanings that contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*): the five consciousnesses are universally acknowledged by the world as direct perception.

Vases, basins, and so forth are universally acknowledged by the world as objects of inference; that is to say, they are known by all to exist after not having existed, and to cease to exist after having existed.

Based on the two absences of the preceding and succeeding moments, one infers that what exists in the interval is impermanent. It is in this sense that [the existence of] speech, sounds, and so forth is established.

Regarding such propositions as "that which is heard" and so forth, or "a jar and the like are eternal," although they are thus established, they are nonetheless rejected by meanings that contradict worldly consensus, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and inference (*anumāna*).
To illustrate with specific examples: to establish that "sound is not audible" contradicts direct perception;
to establish that "jars and the like are eternal" contradicts inference. Question: Why is it that in this context [the contradiction] is specifically...
When it is asked, "Does this refer to existent phenomena? the answer, "and so forth," refers to other items such as jars and basins.

Furthermore, another explanation states that the term "and so forth" in the thesis (*pakṣa*) includes the aforementioned five fallacies, up to the first fallacy: "My mother is a barren woman. Question:
Why are only five of the nine fallacies of the thesis mentioned? Answer: The remaining four fallacies were established by Īśvarasena.
Furthermore, for example, if the *viśeṣya* (the object to be qualified) is not established, this is itself the fault of an unestablished reason (*hetu-asiddha*).

If the *viśeṣaṇa* (the qualifier) is not established, this is itself the fault of lacking a similar instance (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*), as explained previously. If both are not mutually established, this combines the two aforementioned faults;

since those two are not faults, this is also not a fault. This leads to what is called "mutual establishment" (*siddhasādhana*). For example, if one establishes sound as that which is heard, this is fundamentally an unestablished thesis (*asiddha-pakṣa*). Why? [Because it is already established for the proponent.]
As for this: when one establishes a thesis based on false views, it contradicts the opposing thesis; only then does one begin to establish a position (*pakṣa*).

For example, that "sound is what is heard" is something not universally agreed upon—how could such a thing constitute an established thesis? Since there is fundamentally no thesis, whom can one accuse of error?
It is like saying a bhikṣu who exists may be said to have committed a prior offense; but regarding one who is not a bhikṣu, whom can one say has committed an offense? This...

It is also like this. Therefore, there are only five [reasons] that constitute a fault. If one establishes a thesis (*pakṣa*) only after hearing the formal presentation of its contradictory counterpart, why was it previously stated that there are three types of theses, and that even what is "mutually accepted" (*ubhayasiddha*) is called a thesis? Answer:
Regarding "those who [commit] faults regarding the thesis" (*pakṣadoṣa*):
the above has distinguished the faults regarding the correct thesis. From here on, secondly, the faults regarding the false thesis (*mithyā-pakṣadoṣa*) are revealed.

The masters of Hetuvidyā (Logic) and the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhists further establish a sixth category of fault regarding the thesis, termed the "contradictory fault" (*viruddhadoṣa*), because the reason (*hetu*) established contradicts the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Because it contradicts [the thesis], it should also be called the "fallacy of contradicting the reason" (*hetuvirodha*). However, since the thesis was stated first, it is named the "fallacy of contradicting the thesis" (*pratijñāvirodha*).
Now, Dignāga takes up this point and refutes it, stating: "This is not a fallacy of the thesis."
Regarding the phrase "because [it exists] within":

in the treatises on grammar (*śabdavidyā*), there is a formal argument (*prayoga*) in which "sound is eternal" is the thesis (*pakṣa*), "because everything is impermanent" is the reason (*hetu*), and the statement by various masters that "that sound is eternal" is the application (*upanaya*). This is because they take "being entirely impermanent" as the reason.

Because the thesis contradicts the reason, this is the fault of contradicting the thesis (*pratijñā-virodha*). Now, Dignāga takes up [this point] and states that it is a fault of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*) or a fault of the reason (*hetu-doṣa*), and not a fault of the thesis.
This is not the same as the case of the Master Akṣapāda, who established the reason.
This is an illustration used as a skillful means (*upāya*) by one who wishes to establish a distinct property (*anyadharma*).

The statement "all things are impermanent" is the illustration; it is not the reason (*hetu*). The word "its" (*tasya*) is a term belonging to the fifth case (*pañcamī-vibhakti*), which carries the meaning of a reason.
That master of grammatical science (*śabdavidyā-ācārya*) merely employs the door of the reason as a skillful means to establish [the point].

This is an illustration. Therefore, it is said that this is an illustrative expedient (*upāya*). Although an illustration is established as an expedient, one might still erroneously depart from the heterologue (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Consequently, to further establish the heterologue, it is stated above that "this is an illustration," which refers precisely to the heterologue illustration.
Regarding the phrase "by joining the example to show that it is not the case for all":
this reveals that he established the example as a skillful means (*upāya*). Dignāga further used that example to join it with the subject to demonstrate that the reason (*hetu*) exists in the past.
Why is this? For example, if one establishes that sound is permanent, one takes "all things are impermanent" as a dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
Regarding this dissimilar instance, it should be stated: "All impermanent phenomena" refers to all things.

By means of this very dissimilar instance, one conversely reveals and establishes the similar instance (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta); thus, it should be said: "That which is not all things" refers to its nature.
"Permanent. Because of this application through a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one knows that "sound is permanent," taking "not being everything" as the reason (*hetu*).
As for the phrase "this reason is not existent...": [it refers to the fact that the reason is unestablished].
This is not a "non-everything" reason (*asarva-hetu*), as it does not exist within the subject (*pakṣa*).

Since this very sound is included among all things in the world, the property of being "not everything" is not established for either party regarding sound; thus, it is a reason that is unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha-hetu*).
Regarding the phrase "or because it pertains to the meaning":

perhaps they might offer this defense, saying that within sound itself there is also the non-universality of meaning; that is to say, this sound is merely a single sound and does not convey all meanings.
Furthermore, there are cases where the non-universality of meaning serves as the reason. If that were so, then this reason—

This is because it constitutes only one part of that which is to be established (*sādhya*). That is to say, the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established has two parts: the subject (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*).

Since these are expressed by a single word, it is said to be "not all" (*asarva*). If this "not all" is the reason (*hetu*), how does it differ from the word "subject" (*dharmin*) within that which is to be established?
However, the term "not all" refers only to a single property (*dharma*) within the world of conventional expression; thus, it is not the same as [the subject].

The nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is a reason that applies to both [the thesis and the counter-example] and is understood through the analysis of phenomena. However, because it is superior, it is said:

"This is merely a portion of the meaning to be established (*sādhya*); thus, it does not constitute a valid reason (*asiddha-hetu*). Furthermore, this is frequently unestablished (*asiddha*) in both cases. If one considers it from the perspective of its own definition as a reason, it may otherwise be unestablished for either one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*).

Regarding the statement that "this meaning is not established, giving rise to the fault of the reason (*hetu-ābhāsa*)," this does not mean that the meaning of all reasons is unestablished; rather, it refers to the fault of failing to establish the conclusion.
Furthermore, the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) also possesses a fault.
This means that if the reason (*hetu*) is not established simultaneously, it remains unproven; this fault extends even to the example of dissimilar properties (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Regarding the phrase "due to the fault [extending] to the dissimilar," it refers to the fault of inverted exclusion (*viparīta-vyatireka*). One ought to state: "Whatever is impermanent is necessarily all-encompassing," yet the example excludes this statement.

Regarding the phrase "all things": phenomena (*dharma*) are impermanent. As for the meaning of the statement "it is not that they are not all," this refers to a distinction between the subject (*dharmin*), the property (*dharma*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). When it is said "all," this is merely a means of conveying [the point] because they are not actually all;
thus, it is called "all. Here, the upper "not" (*na*) is the means of conveying, while the lower "not-all" is that which is conveyed. By means of this conveyance...

It is not because it refers to all meanings; rather, it is for this reason that it is called "all. That is to say, according to the meaning, when one enters the discourse on principle, the phrase "not what is produced" (*akṛta*) here refers to the textual content concerning that which is unproduced.
"Because the reason (hetu) and the probans (liṅga) are for the most part properties of the thesis (pakṣadharma).

This means that the reason is, in many instances, a property belonging to the subject of the thesis. For example, this includes the six types of inconclusive reasons (anaikāntika), the four types of contradictory reasons (viruddha), as well as correct reasons (saddhetu).

That which is common to both [the subject and the example] is the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*). It is a property belonging to the thesis. Regarding the four types of "unestablished" (*asiddha*):
when a reason is absent from the thesis, it is called "unestablished. Since it is unestablished as a reason, it is not a property belonging to the thesis; therefore, there are only these four types.

There are few remaining [cases of] the indefinite and so forth; because "few" in the sutra implies "many," it is said that "many" refers to the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). The explanation of the text can be understood [thereby].
The verse says: "The property of the subject [exists] in similar instances... (and so on, up to) "...the two."
The "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) refers to the reason (*hetu*) that possesses the nature of being a property of the entire subject. Regarding this reason:

its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) constitutes the first case; its absence from similar instances constitutes the second case; and its presence and absence in similar instances constitute the third case.
In this way, regarding presence and absence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), one likewise formulates three propositions concerning the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Likewise, regarding presence and absence in the similar class, one also formulates three propositions concerning the dissimilar class; that is to say, [the three] are: presence in the similar class, absence in the similar class, and [presence in] both.

Furthermore, regarding both [the "concomitant" and the "non-concomitant"], there are three propositions for each within the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). As stated above, the term "both" (*ubhaya*) is equivalent to the term "and" (*ca*) used below.
These two types of "concomitance" each possess three propositions—namely, existence, non-existence, and both existence and non-existence—resulting in nine varieties in total.
Of these, the first three are: (1) existing in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and also existing in the dissimilar class; (2) existing in the similar class...
[The first] is absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); [the second] is present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*);
[the third] is both present and absent in the dissimilar class. Regarding the second triad: [the first] is absent from the similar class and present in the dissimilar class;
[the second] is absent from the similar class and also absent from the dissimilar class; [the third] is absent from the similar class and both present and absent in the dissimilar class. The third...
Regarding the "three sets of three": first, [the reason] exists in the similar class (sapakṣa) and does not exist in the similar class, yet exists in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa);

second, it exists in the similar class and does not exist in the similar class, yet does not exist in the dissimilar class; third, it exists in the similar class and does not exist in the similar class, yet both exists and does not exist in the dissimilar class.
These shall be explained in detail by citing specific examples in the text below.
Regarding "the true [non-]existence of dharmas":

hereafter, first the two characters *zongfa* (thesis-dharma) are explained. Now, a thesis (*pakṣa*) is defined as the name for the conjunction of the dharma-subject (*dharmin*) and its property (*dharma*).
Regarding the subject (*dharmin*) of the thesis, there are two kinds of properties (*dharma*): first, the unestablished property (*asiddha-dharma*), such as the property of impermanence in sound;

second, the universally established property (*prasiddha-dharma*), such as the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) in sound. This property of being produced must be mutually acknowledged before it can function as a reason (*hetu*) to prove the unestablished property of impermanence.
This is combined with what is universally established. [This concludes] the general entry into the mental verbalization (*vāk-citta*).
Regarding the general function (*samudāyārtha*): one maintains and understands this meaning by first citing the external [position]. The external critique states:

"The establishment of the non-universal function of the mind, as well as the designation of a 'dharma' (property) and its 'dharmin' (substratum) in conjunction, constitutes our present school's position.

Why is it that within the middle school’s intended meaning regarding the basis of these causal dharmas, they do not take the dharma itself, but only take the dharmin? If there were only the dharmin and no taking of the dharma, then... [it would not be established].

It should be called the "proposition" (*pakṣa*). Why, then, does the verse refer to it as the "property of the proposition" (*pakṣadharma*)? Question: The verse mentions only the proposition itself and does not mention the "subject" (*dharmin*).
Why is it that the opponent’s cognition takes the proposition to be the subject, yet does not grasp the property as the means of attainment?
Answer: For example, "sound" is the subject, while "impermanence" and "the nature of being produced" are the properties. These two types of phenomena [are related as follows].
Because they all belong to the category of the subject (*dharmin*), multiple properties do not inherently belong to one another.

Although "sound" and "impermanence" are combined and termed a "thesis" (*pakṣa*), since the verse states that the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), we know that reasons such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) are properties belonging to the subject of the thesis.
In relation to the similar class, these may be present, absent, or both—thus exhibiting three distinct varieties.
The nature of that which is produced as a cause is not a property belonging to the thesis of impermanence,
because the two properties are not related to one another. This is without fault (and so on) regarding the property.
This is the Master of the Treatise’s response. He states that in the verse, the basis for the property of the reason (*hetu*) is simply the subject (*dharmin*) alone;
this is without fault. Why? Because a general term also denotes its particulars. This subject is a collective name;

when one speaks of the "subject" in general, it also denotes its particular instances, namely the properties (*dharma*). Thus, the properties themselves may also be called the "subject," as in the following statement: [text omitted].
"Burning the robe": "robe" (*cīvara*) is a general term. Although "burning the robe" refers to a specific instance, it is also generally referred to as "burning the robe.
This case is likewise: both the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) are collectively termed the "thesis" (*pakṣa*). One may speak of the property-bearer alone as the thesis;

therefore, the thesis upon which the reason's property depends is also called the thesis. Below, he again raises the case of the inverted [reason] together with [the fallacy], or there may be an acceptance.
The treatise states that the term "thesis" (*pakṣa*) refers exclusively to the property of the subject (*dharmadharmatā*), and does not refer to the subject itself (*dharmin*).

Thus, since it is only the property of the subject that is the thesis, it may also be called a "thesis. One should know that the claim that the term "subject" is also called a "thesis" is likewise untenable.
As for the word "thesis," it is simply the name that designates the thesis.
In this context, the "property of the thesis" (pakṣadharma), and so forth, is likewise.
The above has explained the thesis (*pakṣa*); hereafter, the name of the property (*dharma*) is explained. This refers generally to the nature of being a property of the thesis.

That is to say, within this formulation of a thesis, when one intends to take the property of the thesis as the reason (*hetu*), one takes only that which is established and admitted by both the proponent and the opponent.

One takes "the nature of being produced" as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), but does not take "impermanence" as the property of the subject. This is because the proponent (*vādin*) and opponent (*prativādin*) must both agree upon what is established.
Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) of "being produced" must be determined by both parties to be present or absent in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

Regarding the three logical possibilities—presence, absence, and both—of this reason "being produced" within the similar and dissimilar instances, why is it that one speaks only of the "similar instances" and not the "dissimilar instances"? The answer is as follows: [it applies] universally.
This is the reason based on the nature of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*). It is also said to be "mutually admitted" (*sampratipatti*); therefore, it is stated, "it is likewise so.
The following explains the reason why there is mutual admission. Why is this? [From here until] "the cause of arising."
Why must it be said that a reason (*hetu*) can only be established through mutual agreement? There are two kinds of reasons: first, productive causes (*janaka-hetu*);
second, revealing causes (*vyañjaka-hetu*). Here, we rely solely upon the revealing cause for proof. For example, when one establishes that sound is impermanent:
Because it is a product (*kṛtakatva*). This "being a product" must be something definitively accepted by both the proponent and the opponent as being present in the sound;
only then does it constitute a valid reason (*saddhetu*). Why is this so? For example, when one speaks of "being a product," this is the meaning expressed.
It becomes a valid reason only when this meaning is mutually known to exist through the intellectual power of both the proponent and the opponent. Therefore...

This means it is solely by the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*) and so forth. Alternatively, it may mean that by the power of wisdom which knows the cause for both [the proponent and the opponent], one comes to believe and know that there exists this reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), and only then does one understand the meaning of the thesis that sound is impermanent as stated by the proponent.

If the opponent does not believe in the existence of "being produced," they will not comprehend the meaning of the thesis of impermanence. Furthermore, regarding "solely by the power of wisdom," it refers only to...
The opponent understands that there is the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) upon sound;
by virtue of his conviction in the power of that reason (*hetu*), he immediately comprehends the meaning of impermanence (*anitya*) stated by the proponent.

He can also simultaneously comprehend the meaning of the property of being produced as it was stated. Therefore, the subsequent text says: "Because that recollection is based on what is already established for both parties. Thus it is said.

"Unlike [the case of] arising and so forth" means that, for example, just as a seed-opposing condition acts as the cause for the arising of a sprout, it does not become a cause by virtue of being known through intellectual power;

nor does it become a cause simply because it is unknown. Rather, it is solely by virtue of possessing the functional capacity for the seed-opposing condition to produce the sprout that it constitutes the cause;
it does not become a cause depending on whether it is known or unknown. As for what is called a "revealing cause" (*vyañjanahetu*), it necessarily depends on...

Because they are mutually understood, they can then function as causes. Therefore, it is said that they are not like generative causes (*janaka-hetu*), which give rise to an effect through their own power.
If this is so, [then] regarding the formal proposition (*pratijñā*):

Others may object: "If that is so, and cognition is the *jñāpaka-hetu* (probative cause), then since it was previously stated that the 'proof' (*sādhana*) consists of the thesis and other such statements, these multiple statements would themselves produce the meaning of the probandum."
This too [is] well-stated by the Master of the Treatise.
Your objection is not valid. There are three kinds of reasons (*hetu*): first, the reason consisting of the nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth;

second, the cognition (*jñāna*) which is the general designation for the mind and mental factors that know the nature of being produced and so forth; third, [the reason consisting of the nature of being perceived (*upalabhyamānatva*) and so forth].
The phrase "the nature of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth was stated as the logical reason (*hetu*). Now, the proponent clarifies this logical reason:
the opponent recalls that this nature of being produced exists upon the subject (*pakṣa*), namely sound;

it is already established (*prasiddha*) and certain upon similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as a jar, and it is universally absent from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, the opponent has previously accepted its existence; thus, it is termed "established" (*prasiddha*).

However, fearing that the opponent might forget, it is necessary to employ further words; these, combined with the recollection of the originally established meaning, serve as the cause for generating knowledge.
Therefore, within the subject (*dharmin*) of this thesis, one takes only the sense of "possessing the nature of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), which is admitted by both parties as certain.
Regarding its "necessary presence in similar instances" (*sapakṣe sattvam*) and so forth, such an explanation is indeed excellent.
Regarding the phrase "because of this... because of seeing":
if, for this reason, neither the proponent nor the opponent accepts the meaning of this logical reason (*hetu*), then that reason is not established.
This is intended to show by contrast that the reason is only established if both parties must mutually accept the meaning of this reason. Because this [is the case]...

Because of this intention, he proceeds to clarify the fallacy of "non-establishment of both" (*ubhayāsiddha*). This refers to the case where one establishes that sound is impermanent because it is perceived by hearing.
This quality of being "perceived by hearing" is not admitted by either party as a property upon the subject of the thesis, namely sound. Thus, it is non-established for both.
Therefore, it is said that what is accepted by both parties is not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Regarding "the fire exists as a composite":
there are two kinds of fire. The first is fire as a composite of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), such as charcoal fire and the like; this possesses the fire-element of earth (*pṛthivī-tejas*).
The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the fourfold combination are collectively termed "fire. This fire exists or does not exist within mountains, deep places, and so forth.
If intrinsic fire (*svabhāva-agni*) were the only fire element, it would not be called a "combination," and it could not be established that an intrinsic fire element exists.
Since intrinsic fire is experienced in all things, one merely intends to establish the combination of the primary elements.

Fire exists. To explain this according to the superior school that enters into the principle (*yukti*), the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "This mountain, which possesses the four great elements and the four sensory objects, is the *dharmin* (the subject);
'possessing combined fire' is the *dharma* (the predicate). The combination of the *dharma* and the *dharmin* is called the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Because smoke is perceived [as a reason] (*hetu*), it is like a kitchen and so forth [as a similar example] (*sapakṣa*)."
Regarding the phrase "or because [it is] pleasure and so forth":

this is the fourth fault of the unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddha*). The Vaiśeṣika master, in establishing his thesis against a Buddhist disciple, posits that the self (*ātman*) is omnipresent in its essence. The reason that master establishes it in such a manner is because he...
I posit that the self is eternal. Since the self is eternal, the mind lacks the sense of shifting between or maintaining this or that location.
For instance, regarding the experience of this body and world, the meaning of "that which can produce" refers to feelings such as pleasure, which experience things that are agreeable or disagreeable.

The arising of those sensations is likewise the same. Cease, cease! Can it be that the self, as it relies upon this body, moves from these sensations to reach those sensations, such that the experiencer and the objects of pleasure and so forth are distinct? It can only be maintained that the essence of the self is all-pervasive.
Briefly stated, when one enters into successive meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) in various states, there arises the manifestation of activities such as experiencing [objects].
This is just as [one attains] worldly directions in successive lives; this case is likewise.

Therefore, the thesis is that the self (*ātman*) exists as a pervasive entity, because it manifests in all successive births and so forth. However, the disciples of the Buddha do not admit the existence of a self.
Therefore, the *dharmin* (the locus) upon which the reason depends is unestablished (*asiddha*), because there is no *dharmin* available for application.

Furthermore, it is not established as a reason because it does not possess the property of being a *pakṣadharma* (a property of the subject). Thus, it is also an unestablished reason. However, regarding the *dharmin* external [to the debate], within the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), there are only the first two types of non-establishment:
namely, "unestablished for both" (*ubhayāsiddha*) and "unestablished for one or the other" (*anyatarāsiddha*). If it were otherwise, it would be the same as those [other types].
Dharmottara established four types by including those within the two previously mentioned categories of "unestablished" (*asiddha*). That is to say, he divided them into four:

unestablished due to doubt on both sides (*ubhayāsiddha-saṃśaya*), unestablished due to doubt on one side (*anyatarāsiddha-saṃśaya*), unestablished due to the basis being absent on both sides (*ubhayāśrayāsiddha*), and unestablished due to the basis being absent on one side (*anyatarāśrayāsiddha*).
This was done because Dharmakīrti had provided a distinct interpretation for these cases.

Thus, up to the point of "the proponent," the four types of unestablished reasons (*asiddha-hetu*) mentioned above have each been illustrated with specific examples to demonstrate their lack of establishment. Following this same method of explanation,
all other instances of the four types of unestablished reasons regarding any other categories of subjects (*dharmin*) that have been discussed should likewise be understood.
It is not a valid proof (*sādhana*). Furthermore, another explanation states: this summarizes what preceded;
all such statements regarding the four types of unestablished reasons (*asiddha*) across every category are not valid proofs.
Regarding the phrase "up to this point" (*yāvat... iti*) in the statement above:

the preceding section has clarified that the four types of reasons characterized by being properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) constitute the nature of a valid reason (*hetu*). From here on, we shall categorically explain the reason characterized by its necessary presence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*).

This too possesses two [sub-types]: those where it is unestablished in both [similar and dissimilar instances], and those where it is unestablished in either one of the similar instances. For example: [the syllogism]...
The non-establishment of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), the non-establishment of the locus of the similar instance, and the presence, absence, and so forth within that similar instance—
each of these constitutes one of the four types of non-establishment (*asiddha*) as appropriate to the case.
Regarding that which is to be stated [up to] "the refuter":
concerning the reason that is to be stated, this is the correct reason; this is precisely what the subsequent text refers to as "the proof" (*sādhana*).
As for "contradictory and uncertain," this is precisely the "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*) mentioned below. This passage should be stated in full as: "Regarding that which is to be stated as the correct..."
Only within the context of the reason (*hetu*) is there that which is universally accepted as a definitive statement called the "proof" (*sādhana*).

Regarding the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) and the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) which are to be discussed, it is only through a definitive and universally accepted statement that one speaks of the "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*).
How is it that the contradictory and the inconclusive are called refutations? It is because, for the proponent of the thesis (*vādī*), the reason is contradictory.

Regarding the faults of contradiction (*viruddha*) and uncertainty (*anaikāntika*): when an opponent is able to demonstrate that the reason (*hetu*) established by the proponent possesses these faults of contradiction and uncertainty, and this fault is acknowledged as genuine by both the proponent and the opponent, it is termed a "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "because it is not mutually established":
since a refutation is established only through what is commonly accepted by both parties, the fault of "non-establishment for one of the two" constitutes mutual non-establishment.

Mutual non-establishment refers to the reason (*hetu*) being unestablished; it is not a matter of mere verbal expression. Therefore, it cannot definitively determine whether there is proof (*sādhana*) or refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). Thus it is said:
Regarding the phrase "because it must further depend on establishment": consider, for example, the Vaiśeṣika and the Mīmāṃsaka debating whether sound is impermanent.

The Vaiśeṣika establishes that sound is impermanent because it is a product (*kṛtakatva*). However, as for this reason of being a product: if the Vaiśeṣika takes "arising" (*utpatti*) to be the product, then the Mīmāṃsaka’s position is not established;
if the Mīmāṃsaka takes "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) to be the product, then the Vaiśeṣika’s position is not established. Thus, one would have to establish [the reason] yet again.

[Thesis: Furthermore, it is established that sound is in a state of being produced (*janyamāna*). [Reason: Because it changes according to conditions. [Example: Like a lamp flame. This is inconclusive due to doubt.
If one further establishes that fire is definitely absent in that place because smoke exists [there], this is not so;
for wherever there is smoke, there is no fire, just as in other places where there is smoke. Or, it is said:
"There must certainly be fire in that place because smoke is seen nearby, just as in other places where smoke is seen nearby.
[In this case,] both the reason (*hetu*) and the locus (*āśraya*) are unestablished (*asiddha*). Since it is not possible to establish them again, they are not mentioned [separately].

Regarding the phrase "Now, as for 'establishing' (up to) 'what is it?'"—this refers in general to the inquiry of external opponents. Because one employs the method of establishing a thesis (*pakṣa-dharma*), it is called "establishing the thesis-method. Alternatively, because there may be a thesis-property (*dharmin*) and various properties (*dharma*), it is called "establishing the thesis-method.
In principle, this is further explained by the fact that all of these are of the nature of the thesis-property (*pakṣa-dharmatva*).
This establishes the impermanence of the property (dharma) belonging to the subject (pakṣadharma) of this thesis; it does not establish the existence of the subject itself.

This would be inconsistent. If, on the other hand, another causal factor (hetu-dharma) were to establish the mutual existence of the subject as being existent, or if the establishment of the subject as existent were sufficient, I shall further point out the matter below. For example, it is like the Sāṃkhya school establishing that the Primal Matter (pradhāna) is existent. This...

There exists a supreme entity (*dharmas*). We now establish that this entity exists (the thesis). This is because we observe that distinct individual things possess a general category (*sāmānya*) (the reason).
It is just as, for example, many pieces of white sandalwood are all [categorized] by their source (the analogy).

One should know that while the twenty-three principles (*tattvas*) are distinct, there is likewise a general, supreme, and all-pervading purity (*viśuddhi*). If one were to establish it as non-existent, [the Buddha’s] younger brother...
The son then establishes that "the most excellent" (*jyeṣṭha*) is non-existent. [Thesis: That which is the most excellent is a non-existent phenomenon (*asaddharma*).

[Reason: Because it is unapprehendable (*anupalabdhi*). [Example: Just like the horns of a rabbit (*śaśaviṣāṇa*). In this manner, one establishes the existence of a phenomenon by means of other reasons and phenomena.
That which is thus established is not the doctrine of our own school, as it contradicts correct reasoning. [The opponent] asks: "What is the meaning of this?
In this context, what is this fault? [The response continues: "In this... up to "...this fault."

When the treatise reaches the point of demonstrating the reason for establishing what is most excellent regarding existence and non-existence, it simply posits that, among the twenty-three truths (*satya*), distinct entities are existent.
That which is determined to exist as a single cause is a phenomenon (*dharma*); this single cause that exists is precisely the most excellent.

Regarding the twenty-three truths (*tattva*) as the subject (*dharmin*), one establishes that the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*) exists as a distinct entity. However, one does not establish the Supreme Lord himself as the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Therefore, there is no fallacy of using a property (*dharma*) to establish the existence of the subject (*dharmin*). The formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: [Thesis]: Among these, the twenty-three truths are distinct entities;
they must necessarily possess at least one cause [as their creator] (the thesis). [Reason]: Because they are distinct entities (the reason). [Example]: Just like many pieces of white cloth.
[The example is] the same as the donor (*dāna*).

If it is argued that there is the fault of establishing [something] as non-existent (*abhāva*), then if one establishes the "supreme" (*parama*) as non-existent, this too is based on the twenty-three truths (*tattva*); it is by way of these that the supreme is conventionally established as non-existent. This is because...
Because it cannot be apprehended. To establish the formal argument (*pramāṇa*), one says: "The twenty-three principles (*tattva*) have no single supreme cause" (the thesis);
"because a supreme [cause] cannot be apprehended" (the reason); "just like a rabbit's horn" (the concordant example). Furthermore, another explanation states:

If one were to establish [the supreme cause] as non-existent, then that which is designated as existent—such as the so-called *śiva* or *prakṛti*—is a subject of existence (*dharmin*). I now establish it as follows:

There is no such dharma. Both "dharma" and "existent dharma" are designated as the thesis (*pakṣa*). Furthermore, regarding the refutation of the conception of a supreme entity, this is also provisionally established;

because it is unobtainable, it serves as the reason (*hetu*). Since I now establish that the supreme existent dharma is the thesis of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is likewise no fault of having a supreme existent dharma.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: Your [position]...

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that "the most excellent [self] exists. The reason (*hetu*) is "because it is unapprehendable. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like a rabbit's horn. Question: Why is this not a valid reason?

It lacks the basis (*āśraya*). Answer: There are three types of reasons. First, there are reasons that must pertain only to an existent entity (*bhāva*), such as the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).
For example, one might say: "Space is a real entity because it is the substratum (*āśraya*) of real qualities. This is such a reason.
Since it relies solely upon an existent dharma (*dharmin*), it is a "non-establishment of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*) in relation to non-existence.

If a Mahāyāna proponent were to establish [a reason] against the Hīnayāna, non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), and so forth—since these groups do not admit the existence of the eighth consciousness—it would likewise be a "non-establishment of the locus" because the *dharmin* (the subject) is not established for them when arguing against the non-existence of the eighth consciousness. This too is a case of the "non-establishment of the locus."
This is not established. Second, there may be a reason that relies solely upon non-existence (*abhāva*), namely, because it is unapprehendable (*anupalabdhi*).

Here, we clarify that the reason of unapprehensibility relies solely upon the most excellent non-existence; for it is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) established upon the nature of dharmas with respect to the conceptualization of dharmas as having intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, there would be the fault that a cause would lack a basis, as it would not exist without a cause. Thirdly, some causes apply to both existence and non-existence;

for example, the nature of being produced (*kṛtaka*) and so forth. Therefore, if one establishes a positive phenomenon (*bhāva*) as existing, the opponent will certainly not admit that the phenomenon exists.
Thus, when debating with one who maintains a negative phenomenon (*abhāva*), the reason (*hetu*) necessarily commits the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). If one establishes...
There are phenomena that are non-existent. If such phenomena are established as non-existent, although an opponent may not grant this, it nonetheless cannot be found;
for the reason (hetu) relies solely upon a non-existent phenomenon. Thus, there is no fault of the basis being unestablished (āśrayāsiddha), because that which does not exist serves as the basis.
This is like addressing a non-Buddhist: "The self (ātman) is non-existent" (the thesis); "because it cannot be found" (the reason); "just like the horns of a rabbit" (the concordant example).
[Analogy]. Although this reason lacks a basis, it is nonetheless free from fault.
As for the question "How so?", the opponent asks:
"In the correct principle of establishing a reason, since the nature of the basis is the property of the reason, how can [the thesis] be established?"

This is the constant principle of the *dharmin* (the subject). Now, the treatise poses a question: "If one posits another *dharmin* by means of a *dharmin*, or establishes its property (*dharma*) by means of a *dharmin*, what is the illustration of this?
To point to the matter at hand, it cites a fallacious syllogism: "Smoke possesses fire; smoke is the *dharmin*;
fire is its *dharma* (the thesis); because it is smoke (the reason); just like [the smoke] in a kitchen (the example). However, as for the smoke...
Fire and smoke are both *dharmas* (phenomena). That person establishes the *dharma* of fire as the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) by means of the *dharma* of smoke.
This mind does not take [the subject] itself as a *dharma* to establish another *dharma*.

As for the statement that "fire establishes tangibility," fire is a *dharma* consisting of the four sense objects (*viṣaya*) conventionally designated as fire; the term "tangibility" refers to the *dharma* of hot touch.
Alternatively, one might formulate a syllogism as follows: "This fire possesses the quality of hot touch (the thesis), because it is a fire (the reason), just like other fires (the example).
Does this [syllogism] establish a property of a subject that does not exist? The opponent does not understand these two meanings.
Therefore, as for what its meaning is:
regarding the phrase "now, in relation to the object," the Master of the Treatise replies: "In this present system, fire is not established by means of smoke as the reason."

It is not by means of smoke as the locus (*dharmin*) that fire is established as the locus; nor is it by taking fire as the reason (*hetu*) that tactile contact is established as the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Rather, by means of the four sensory objects collectively assumed as the locus of fire, one establishes the specific, substantial dharma of tactile contact.
Regarding the statement, "merely for the purpose of establishing this associated entity": it means that one merely establishes this smoke and the locus of touch;
there is no associated entity [apart from them]. For example, as in the formal inference (*prayoga*): "In this mountain valley there is fire.

Here, the four elements (*catuṣ-ṛtu*) of the mountain valley constitute the *dharmin* (the subject), and the presence of fire constitutes the *dharma* (the predicate). The combination of the *dharma* and the *dharmin* forms the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Because there is smoke in this mountain valley (the reason), it is like other places where there is smoke (the example). Furthermore, one may formulate a syllogism as follows:
There is the sensation of heat at this hearth (the thesis), because there is fire (the reason), just like other places where there is fire (the example).

If [the reason] "not reaching" (*aprāpti*) were not the cause, the Master of the Treatise would refute the previous erroneous formulation: "If it were not as I have stated, then the inference (*anumāna*) could be established as you have proposed."
One should therefore take a portion of the thesis (*pakṣa*) itself as the reason (*hetu*). For example, if one establishes the thesis: "Sound is impermanent.

Here, "sound" is the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and "impermanence" is the property (*dharma*). Both the property and the property-bearer constitute the meaning of the thesis to be established. If one were to say:
"Sound is impermanent (thesis), because it is sound (reason)," this would be a case where the property-bearer within the thesis is used as the reason; therefore, it is [fallacious].
Regarding the two parts of the thesis (*pakṣa*): you fall into the fault of using one part as the reason (*hetu*). It is just like this: you previously formulated the syllogism as follows:
"Smoke" is the subject (*dharmin*), and "fire" is the property (*dharma*). The combination of the property and the subject constitutes the thesis.
Yet, when you establish the reason, saying "because it is smoke," is this not taking one part of the thesis—the subject—as the reason? Furthermore, you established...
The *Pramāṇa* states: "This fire possesses the quality of hot touch. Here, "fire" is the subject (*dharmin*), and "hot touch" is the property (*dharma*).
