The combination of these two parts—the property and the subject—constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*). To establish the reason (*hetu*), one says, "Because it is great.
This also fails to be established because it uses a portion of the subject of the thesis as its own reason; for both parts of the thesis are that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
Because the reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes [the thesis], one should not take a portion of the probandum (*sādhya*) as the means of establishment.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it exists," the Master of the Treatise (Vasubandhu) again refutes this. Moreover, in this inference, it is not intended to establish that fire is the property of the subject (*dharmin*).
Furthermore, heat and touch possess existence, because fire and touch are universally known by the world to have substantial natures.

What is meant by "establishing"? This would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*). However, for those who do not understand the characteristics of fire and touch, it is necessary to establish that there is fire and touch in the locus where they reside;
thus, one speaks of establishing through formal inference (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding "one who has a fault" (yāvad-doṣavān):
moreover, in this context, the proponent of a thesis must depend upon the opponent's position in order for their own thesis to be established.
For example, when a follower of the Buddha wishes to establish that sound is impermanent, they must depend upon the opponent. To establish [this],...
Because sound is eternal, one establishes impermanence as both the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and the locus of that property (*dharmin*).
Since not everyone can ascertain whether there is fire or no fire beneath the smoke, and since fire is also hot, how could the sense organ itself constitute the thesis (*pakṣa*)?

If one must depend upon something else to establish what is to be proven, it is not like the Vaiśeṣika categories of substance (*dravya-pada*) and quality (*guṇa-pada*), which do not [require such dependence].

It is established through mutual dependence. To say that "there is a locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) refers to the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*), because it possesses the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*).
The category of quality is that which belongs [to the substance]. One should not say that the quality exists in the same manner as the possessor of the quality.

Regarding the verse on the *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition), up to the phrase "the subject possessing the property" (*dharmin*), this reiterates the verse concerning the "subject" (*pakṣa*). It explains the meaning of the preceding verse.

When it says "the subject possessing the property is not that which establishes the subject possessing the property," it means that one should not establish the existence of fire as the subject possessing the property by means of smoke as the subject possessing the property. As for the phrase "and the property" (*dharma*), it likewise means that one should not [establish the subject] by means of fire...
There is a *dharmin* (subject). This establishes the nature of contact (*sparśa*). Since that hot contact is a partial attribute (*ekadeśārtha*) of fire, it is a *dharma* (predicate).
The five characters "its phrase," "upper," "middle," and "upper" penetrate this *dharma*, as well as the character "and" (*ca*) and the character "it.
To say "this does not establish a *dharmin*" means that this *dharma* should not be established as a *dharmin*. This refers to the preceding text. By means of...
Other distinct dharmas establish [the subject] as being either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The latter two lines state the correct meaning (*samyagartha*):

that is, by means of the property of the reason (*hetudharma*), one establishes the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*). Since such a dharma and its substratum (*dharmin*) are not mutually exclusive, it also constitutes the substratum itself.
This is the correct meaning, because it is understood that the reason has a basis. Thus, by means of the dharma...
When the property (*dharma*) is established, it simultaneously establishes the locus (*dharmin*). One cannot establish the locus by means of the property alone;
for if there were [a locus] such that the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) exists...

The property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) is of two kinds. First, a property not universally established (*aprasiddha*): for example, "impermanence in sound," because it is not accepted by the proponents of sound (*śabdavādin*).
This is called the "property of the thesis" because this thesis itself is the property. Second, a universally established property (*prasiddha*): namely, "the nature of being produced in sound.

Because this is accepted only by the opponent (*prativādin*), it is the property belonging to the proponent (*vādin*) in this thesis; thus it is named the "property of the thesis. The above establishes the reason (*hetu*) that clarifies the subject matter.
Regarding "dharma": within a given thesis (*pakṣa*), that which exists upon it is called the "dharma of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*).

Now, since Dignāga has composed this treatise, all instances from the ancient *hetuvidyā* (logic) where a formal inference (*prayoga*) was established with implicit elements have been explained by citing the words of various scholars.
Thus, he cites the position of an opponent, such as a Vaiśeṣika, who, addressing a Śabdika, establishes a thesis (*pakṣa*) stating: "Sound is not eternal. He then states the reason (*hetu*).
It says: "Because karma and so forth would have to be eternal. This refers to the third category of karma (*karmapada*), namely walking, coming, bowing, looking up, and so on.
The phrase "and so forth" includes the second category of qualities (*guṇapada*), which indicates the teaching of the Dharma. This is the reason why karma and so forth would have to be eternal:

[the claim] that this third category of karma must be eternal is not supported by the second category of qualities, such as the voice. This, then, contradicts the intended meaning of the thesis (*siddhānta*).
Regarding the "property" (*dharma*): how can it be said that because it is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), it is called the "property of the thesis" (*paksadharma*)?
Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is established as: "because it ought to be perceived at all times. This means that this sound ought to be heard at all times;

such a sense of "ought to be perceived at all times" does not exist within the sound itself. This is something neither [the proponent] nor [the opponent] admits, for the sound is not perceived at all times.

The middle [term] is always obtainable by the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). From this, it follows that what is separately clarified must be separately obtained; it has no connection with the matter of sound.
May it be called the "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*)? Or is it further named the "thesis-property" (*siddhāntadharma*)?
Regarding this statement [extending] "this explains the fault of that," the commentary says:
This is the master of the treatise’s resolution of the objection. This is the Vaiśeṣika doctrine; it is the fault of the Śabdika (Proponent of Sound).
This is because, by way of the cause (*hetu*) as the door and by way of the thesis (*pakṣa*) as the door, the proponent first establishes what is to be proven, and then the opponent speaks.

One should say that it is difficult [to refute]. It demonstrates that [if sound were eternal], it would have to be eternal; this is because it is stated as something that ought to be said. Therefore, one knows that this is a statement intended to point out the opponent's fault.

This is because the earlier masters of the Śabdika school, in opposition to the Vaiśeṣikas, established the thesis (*pakṣa*) that "sound is eternal" with the reason (*hetu*) that "it lacks material form."
It is like empty space (the corroborative example). Later, the Vaiśeṣika school refutes that error by means of the categories of cause (*hetu*) and thesis (*pakṣa*).

If you say that sound is eternal because it lacks material form as its cause, then the third category, action (*karman*), and so forth, which also lack material form, should likewise be eternal. Furthermore, you previously established the thesis that sound is eternal.
Now, furthermore, according to that school’s own tenets, they refute this by saying: "If sound were permanent, it should be apprehended by the auditory consciousness as something permanent.
Since it is now commonly observed that non-permanent sound is apprehended by the auditory consciousness, we know that sound is not permanent."
"If it is thus... (up to) what is it?
This further raises an external counter-example: for instance, as when the Vaiśeṣika school, in opposition to the Śabdika school, establishes the thesis that sound is impermanent.
The fact that what is produced is impermanent serves as a reason; the fact that what is permanent is not produced serves as a reason.
Since these two reasons are both not [present] in the world, how can one say that because it is a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), it is called a "property of the thesis"?
Therefore, it is asked: "How is this so?"
This is an illustration [extending] to the term "causeless.
From this point downward, the Master’s formal argument (*pramāṇa*) applies to all cases, such as "that which is produced is impermanent," and so forth.

It is not that the reason (*hetu*) itself is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*); rather, by relying on the fifth case (the ablative), the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is established as the reason for the sound through a skillful means (*upāya*).

Because it is produced (*kṛtaka*). That is to say, whatever is produced by a phenomenon is not eternal, such as a jar or a basin; these are the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
If a phenomenon were eternal, one would have to say that [the reason] is not a cause or an example; however, it is not eternal.
"Like space," and so forth, are examples by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), which are to be applied according to their respective order.

To proclaim the reason as necessarily following from the thesis (*pakṣa*)—as a calf follows its mother—is an example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), because that which is produced is impermanent.
If the thesis were absent where the reason is absent, it would lack a reason; therefore, since that which is permanent is not produced, it is called an example by dissimilarity.
Regarding the phrase "because within this [context]...
the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*): these two examples do not actually possess the property of the subject upon the sound.

Nevertheless, by means of the application in the similar example (*sapakṣa*) within this context, they skillfully demonstrate that the reason (*hetu*), namely "the state of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), exists upon the sound. This is what is meant by "the property."
That which is produced is impermanent. Since sound is a product, it is therefore impermanent.
Although the proponent of the thesis does not explicitly state this application (*upanaya*) in the text, such an application is nonetheless implied.
Thus, by means of the application and the example, it is demonstrated that sound is necessarily a product; it is not the case that it is not a product.
Therefore, this property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is definitively a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); thus it is called a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).
Regarding the statement in the *Pramāṇa* [treatise] that leads to the knowledge of the reason (*hetu*):

the first line of this root verse corresponds to the previously mentioned similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and the second line corresponds to the previously mentioned dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). This is based on the fifth [chapter].

Regarding "the explicit illustration" (*udāharaṇa*): the illustration is the first turning [of the wheel]. As stated previously: "Because that which is produced is impermanent; because that which is not produced is [permanent].
Here, the word "because" (*hi*) concludes the illustrative reason (*hetu-dharma*). This is the fifth sound, the "supporting reason" (*hetu-dhāraṇa*).

Based on this fifth supporting reason, one states the similar and dissimilar illustrations; therefore, it is called the "explicit illustration. As for the statement, "By means of the application (*upanaya*), one knows the reason":
Through the positive application of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the negative exclusion of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), one comes to know the reason (*hetu*).

This refers to manifesting the example by means of the word "reason," and manifesting the reason by means of the example. Furthermore, another interpretation states: if one relies on the five-membered syllogism, it is as follows:
[Thesis: Sound is impermanent; [Reason: Because it is a product; [Example: Whatever is a product is impermanent, such as a jar and so forth; [Application: Since sound is...

[The example] "that which is produced" [serves as the concordant instance]. Therefore, it is impermanent [the conclusion]. Now, regarding the statement that the reason is known through the application (*upanaya*):
it is because of the fourth member, the application, that one knows the reason—namely, the state of being produced—in relation to sound.

Although the reason is not explicitly stated in the text, the thesis is understood by the wise through the application; therefore, it is not mentioned. This was stated by Dignāga, the master of the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic).
It is said: the fourth [member], "conjunction" (*yukti*), is the statement of the second reason (*hetu*); the fifth, "conclusion" (*nigamana*), is the statement of the first thesis (*pakṣa*).
Furthermore, two parts are subsumed under the former [thesis], and three parts are subsumed under the former [reason].
Regarding the phrase "from this [point] to the digression":
by means of the preceding three analogies, both positive and negative, the thesis is established; that is, the Sāṃkhya system has already been refuted.
Specifically, the method of establishing a thesis through a negative analogy alone is not successful. For example, as the Sāṃkhya says: "There is a self within the internal body" (the thesis).

Because it is capable of moving and shaking and possesses consciousness (the reason), that which cannot move and shake and lacks consciousness—such as a tree (the dissimilar example)—must certainly be without a self.

Since there is no positive concordant example, one establishes the existence of a self within the internal body by employing the method of the negative dissimilar example, which refutes its absence. Below...

The *Jiyao lun* (Treatise on the Essential Points) sets forth two types of examples: because the reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is observed in the category of the impermanent and not observed in the category of the permanent, it is only when these two examples are complete that the thesis is established.
The Vaiśeṣika addresses the Śabdika, saying: "In this way, I establish that sound is not eternal; for if it were eternal, it would necessarily not be something produced."
Thus, having established the *sādharmya* (conformity) and the two types of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), one is finally able to provide the *niścita-śeṣa* (the remainder that is determined).

Therefore, the *sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta* establishes [the conclusion], while the *vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta* refutes [the contrary]. These two methods of exemplification both serve toward a single *niścita-śeṣa*.
This is not like the Sāṃkhya school, which relies solely on the *vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta* as a means of refutation to produce a distinct determination.

This establishes the remaining reasons. Just as I refuted the Sāṃkhya school by employing only the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) to establish the existence of a self (*ātman*), thereby subverting their expedient reasons;
so too have I composed the *Sāṃkhyakhaṇḍana*, a treatise of six thousand verses, which I have already explained in detail.
The Sāṃkhya school establishes only the method of refutation through counter-argument (*prati-prasanga*) in order to distinguish the faults in their reasons (*hetu*).
For now, I shall cease this extensive refutation of other systems within this treatise. The founder of the Sāṃkhya school was the Sage Kapila;
his original name was *Kapila*, which means "yellow. He was so called because the hair on his head and face was yellow. The older transcription "Kāpila" is a corruption of the sound.

This master established the doctrine of the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*). Having finished entrusting it to his devoted disciple, he intended to enter the Truth (*tattva*). The disciple entreated him, saying:
"Master, you should remain in this world permanently. If there are those in later generations who do not believe in the twenty-five principles," [may you stay to teach them].
He manifested his form to preach for them, so that his teaching might be practiced perpetually. The Master said, "So be it.
He then transformed a large stone into lapis lazuli, about several *zhang* in size, and concealed himself within it. Whenever someone requested his presence, he would manifest his form at that time.
Later, when Dignāga appeared in the world, he composed the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*. His disciple did not wish to refute [the Sāṃkhya teacher] himself, but instead deferred to his master.
Dignāga went to the place where the stone was, wrote upon it a refutation of the doctrine of the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*), and sealed it over with the stone.
After one night had passed, [the teacher] surely attempted to defend it again; Dignāga refuted it once more. When [the teacher] could no longer defend it, he finally emerged [to meet him].
Treatise: Such establishment and refutation comprise six thousand verses, which fully refute the twenty-five principles (pañcaviṃśati-tattva). At that time, the stone roared loudly.
What is now referred to as "refuting the Sāṃkhya" points to those six thousand verses composed by him to refute the Sāṃkhya treatise.
Regarding the "proponent's property" (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth up to the "thesis" (*pakṣa*):

there are two types of proponent's properties. First, the non-universally established property (*aprasiddhadharma*), such as the property of impermanence in sound. Second, the universally established property (*prasiddhadharma*).

This refers to the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) residing in sound. Now, by restating the property already established through the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*), it becomes the "reason-property" (*hetudharma*).
Therefore, it is called "such a property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*). This reason has three types of distinctions:

first, its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*); second, its absence from similar instances; and third, its presence and absence both within similar instances. Therefore, it is said that "both [apply]."
If the word "and" (ca) were not included, there would be a fear that it might mean either "existence" or "non-existence" alone; thus, for the time being, it is treated as "only" (eva).
If the word "and" were placed [there], then one would expect that in addition to existence and non-existence, there would separately be their "conjunction" (ubhaya).

However, in the previous verse, it was stated only that the property of the subject exists in the similar instances as "existent," "non-existent," or "both. Because the verse was concise, the word "and" was omitted from the previous verse; it is now supplied here.
"It is placed within the [section on] 'application' (prayoga). Regarding the phrase 'herein... as for the dissimilar instance' (*vipakṣa*):
since the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) has already been analyzed above, what follows below merely explains the term 'similar instance' (*sapakṣa*). As for the word 'herein' (*atra*):"
Regarding the term "category" (*pakṣa*) within the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*): "category" refers to a distinct class, such as a jar, sound, and so forth;

it is the distinct category that serves as the basis for the property of the subject, namely impermanence. As for the statement that what is "similar to the category" (*sapakṣa*) is that which is proximate to and equal to the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*):
if the category of jars possesses impermanence, it is similar to the impermanent property predicated of sound; therefore, each [is called a similar instance].
Because they are proximate and equal, a jar is said to be of the same class (*sapakṣa*). This is because all meanings of "entity" (*bhāva*) are designated as distinct classes.
If [the property of] impermanence were not established upon the dharmas that constitute distinct classes such as space (*ākāśa*), [it would not be a valid reason].
This is called the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*). Regarding the phrase "not [being] with...

or different," the following section cites and refutes the views of ancient masters. There were differing explanations by two ancient masters of the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) school regarding the definition of the term "dissimilar instance. First:
The Master said: "For example, if one establishes that sound is impermanent, taking jars and the like as similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and space and the like as dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

When, upon those [dissimilar instances] such as space, there is something that contradicts and harms the thesis (*pakṣa*), or when there is something on the similar instances that contradicts impermanence, this is called 'contradiction' (*viruddha*).
This contradiction is termed a 'dissimilar instance' (*vipakṣa*), just as enemies who harm one another are called 'contradictory. This continues until [the point of] warmth."
Taking this as the thesis (*pakṣa*), "being a means of expression" (*vācakatva*) is considered a contradictory property and thus termed "dissimilar" (*vipakṣa*). The second master says:
For example, when it is established that sound is impermanent (*anitya*), everything other than what is not impermanent is called the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

Now, according to our own author [Dignāga], if there is no location where the thesis to be established—impermanence—is absent, that is called the dissimilar instance; this differs from the first master’s view regarding the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

This is incorrect. Because the latter master’s position differs from the [proponent’s] thesis (*pakṣa*), it is called the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, it is said that it is neither contradictory to nor different from the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
If it were contradictory, it would follow that it should be excluded solely as a distinct category.
[Thesis: It follows that there is further heat here, [Reason: because there is fire, [Example:
just as in a kitchen where there is fire, there is invariably heat; whereas in all places where there is no fire, there is likewise no heat. This is the correct formulation.
If one were to say: "This place has heat (the thesis), because there is fire (the reason), just like a kitchen (the example); whereas where there is cold, there is no fire, such as on Mount Meru;

since this [latter] possesses cold, it contradicts the presence of heat and thus serves as a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta)," then this should merely serve to distinguish the dissimilar example from the similar example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta). Its function is simply to differentiate the dissimilar case.
How can an analogy not necessarily demonstrate that the thesis follows from the reason? What is the case here?

If, in relation to a "warm" thesis, one uses "cold," which contradicts warmth, as a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), then regarding those places that are neither cold nor warm, it is unknown whether they definitely belong to the class of the [probandum].

Even if there were a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) of something warm, in those places that are neither cold nor warm, there would simply be no fire. This is based on the principle of contradiction.
For example: wherever there is cold, there is no fire; yet in a neutral place, since it is not cold, there must likewise be fire.
This counter-example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) conversely implies that fire exists, thereby establishing the fallacy of the reason being inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Is it like a kitchen where heat exists because fire is present? Or is it like a neutral place where, despite the presence of fire, there is no heat?
Yes. Because the cause for fire is not certain, it cannot definitively prove the presence of heat.

If one does not rely on its contradiction with the presence of heat, but instead uses "the presence of [something else]" as the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), then there would be no fault of the cause for fire being uncertain.
If one were to say that wherever there is no fire, there is also no heat, then as for that location...
Therefore, there is no fire in the locus of the neutral middle term (*madhyama-pakṣa*), as these are all instances of a dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Now, regarding the reason "because it possesses heat" for the presence of fire, one must certainly maintain that this reason for the presence of fire is free from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
"If it were distinct, there would be no cause.

Below this, the second teacher's position is refuted. If you claim that something is a "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*) simply because it differs from the thesis (*pakṣa*), then there would be no definitive correct reason (*saddhetu*).
Why? For example, when one establishes that sound is impermanent, [the property of] being selfless (*anātman*) within sound [would also be a dissimilar instance].

That which differs from the thesis of impermanence constitutes the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Now, the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) exists within the meaning of this dissimilar instance, namely "selflessness.
If that were so, this reason would be an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*), because it exists in the dissimilar instance.
Since a reason must exist only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and be absent from the dissimilar instances, such a determinate reason does not exist here.
Regarding the phrase "because it contradicts [the opposite]" (*virodhāt*):
since there is no locus for that which is established, this is the principle of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

Thus, the reason (*hetu*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) can correctly establish impermanence, while incidentally establishing selflessness (*anātman*) and suffering (*duḥkha*); hence the word "etc. (*ādi*). For example, as when one says, "Sound is selfless."
Because it is a product, like a jar and so forth. This also establishes that sound is non-self (*anātman*), because the property of being a product does not contradict the thesis of non-self;

furthermore, since non-self and impermanence are not mutually exclusive in their characteristics, they may both equally take "being a product" as the logical reason (*hetu*). Why? Because sound possesses no permanent self.
Because it is attained, one may say it is impermanent, and one may also say it is non-self; for all impermanent phenomena are devoid of self.

Therefore, there is no contradiction. This intention is intended to clarify that the locus where phenomena are impermanent is termed the "dissimilar instance" (vipakṣa), whereas their lack of self cannot be so termed.
For even sound itself is non-self; it is not something separate from non-self.

[The reason] "because it exists in that which is always present" [is established] even with respect to selflessness. Furthermore, another explanation is as follows: the probans consisting of the nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) can correctly establish impermanence;

it is not the case that it is a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) by virtue of having a contradictory character, because such a [contradictory] instance cannot correctly establish [the opposite]. Why is this?
For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced. Here, space and so forth, which are permanent, constitute the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) by virtue of being contradictory.
This contradictory dissimilar instance cannot correctly demonstrate that sound is impermanent, because the reason (*hetu*) is not excluded from it.
That is to say, the reason still exists even in non-contradictory things such as rabbit horns. According to my interpretation, however...
That which is not the locus of the thesis is called the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*). This also serves to exclude that [probandum] from the reason.

That is to say, it demonstrates that the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is precisely what establishes impermanence. The property of being produced is precisely what establishes impermanence.

If the property of being produced were to establish impermanence only incidentally, it would not differ from the latter master’s position, because it would be distinct from the thesis (*pakṣa*); therefore, it is called "dissimilar."

If it differs from the thesis (*pakṣa*), it is called the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Up to the point of "selflessness," it also differs from "impermanence," and thus it is likewise a dissimilar instance.
Within all dissimilar instances, there is no such thing as the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). If that is so, then regarding the reason (*hetu*) of the property of being produced:

Thus, it cannot serve as collateral evidence for selflessness. According to my interpretation, wherever the probandum (the property to be proven) is absent, the reason (the logical mark) is entirely non-existent;
the sound is likewise a case where the probandum is absent, because whatever is impermanent is necessarily without a self.

Therefore, the reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) can also incidentally establish selflessness (*anātman*). Regarding the statement that there is no contradiction, it is the same as the two previous interpretations.
As for the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes the [four] bases (*āyatana*); this is because the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is not [self], yet it is of the nature of being produced.
Regarding the phrase "if a phenomenon (up to) resembles the cause," this raises the fault of a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*).
It demonstrates that there is no error in using "the state of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) to prove impermanence, nor in its incidental establishment of [properties] such as non-self (*anātman*).
The term "if a phenomenon" refers to the phenomenon that serves as the reason (*hetu-dharma*). If the reason were able to establish something contradictory...

Regarding "the proponent": for example, when one asserts that the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another, using "the nature of being an aggregate" as the reason (*hetu*) and "bedding" as the corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Now, the reason—namely, the nature of being an aggregate—is established by the word [itself], and the subject to be established (*sādhya*) is the eyes and so forth.
It must be for the purpose of accumulation for another; this very "accumulation for another" is what is established [as the thesis].
Since this established point directly contradicts the previously stated thesis that "it is not for the purpose of accumulation for another," it is called "contradictory.
Because the reason of "the nature of being accumulated" serves as the cause for this contradictory establishment, it is said that "if a dharma can establish a contradiction."
What has been established is as follows: this is the fallacy of contradiction, known as a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
The statement "as it is with non-contradictory [reasons], so it is with contradictory ones" points out the fallacy of contradiction.
That is to say, the Sāṃkhya school originally established that "necessarily existing for the sake of another" is their primary tenet. Because...

The nature of being an accumulation (*saṃcita*) is the primary reason (*hetu*). The original thesis (*pakṣa*) established is called "non-contradictory" (*avirodhin*), because this reason of accumulation is precisely capable of establishing that non-contradictory thesis; thus, it is termed the "non-contradictory reason.

This reason of the nature of accumulation not only establishes the non-contradictory thesis, but also incidentally establishes that the eyes and so forth must necessarily serve another purpose through their state of being accumulated. This very...
"Accumulation for the sake of another" means that this very accumulation is for the sake of another; this is what is established [by the opponent].

This contradicts the previously stated thesis (*pakṣa*) that "it must necessarily be for the sake of another," and is therefore called a contradiction (*viruddha*). In this way, obtaining the [opponent's] thesis is termed a contradiction;
one should know that the previous thesis is termed "non-contradictory" because it is not so obtained.
Regarding the phrase "because the property to be established has no fixed existence," this expresses the same principle as what was previously stated.

That is to say, for example, if one were to establish the thesis that "the eyes and so forth must exist as something other than an accumulation," using "the nature of being an accumulation" as the reason (*hetu*),
[this reason] would necessarily exist in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) but would not be accepted in the absence of the property to be established.

It is entirely absent from the category [of the subject]. Now, the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) is likewise: that is to say, the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established must necessarily be for the sake of another through accumulation;
yet, in no place does the cause of its accumulated nature exist, because it is definitively non-existent.

To say that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) does not exist is precisely that the thesis to be established is non-existent—namely, that it must necessarily be for the sake of another through accumulation. "Because it is definitively non-existent" means:

This is because the cause for the nature of being an accumulation does not exist. To say "the cause for the nature of being an accumulation" is able to establish the prior non-contradictory thesis (*asādhya-pakṣa*) and is entirely absent from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
Now, the contradictory thesis (*viruddha-pakṣa*) is also established, and it too is entirely absent from dissimilar instances; therefore, it is said to be "likewise."
This is a truly contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*). Below, the indeterminate (*anaikāntika*) is cited to demonstrate that it is not a contradictory reason.

Regarding the phrase "because [it] exists," this refers to the reason of being an aggregate (*saṃghātatva*), which can establish the property of being for the sake of another (*parārthatva*). This reason is determinate; it is not like [the case of] a jar or similar objects.

Because the reason (*hetu*) is indeterminate (*anaikāntika*). Why? For example, if one establishes that sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar or similar things, someone might object: "Sound must be a jar, because it is produced, just like a jar.

This reason thus possesses the fallacy of being indeterminate, resulting in doubt, because [the property of being produced] exists among those [things] through a series of intermediate steps. That is to say, if...
Sound being a jar, a cloth, and so forth, constitutes the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). This property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) exists both in jars and in cloths.
Alternatively, one might raise the objection: "Sound must be a cloth, because it is produced, just like a cloth.
In this case, only the cloth is the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), while jars and the like are the dissimilar instances. This property of being produced [exists] in the absence of a cloth...
Because it exists upon things such as pots; because it is said that there is no intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) through successive transmission;

and because the reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) exists within the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), this first interpretation is not certain. Regarding the second [interpretation], it further states:
this text follows upon the preceding correct reason (*saddhetu*); that is to say, by virtue of the preceding "being produced," one can establish impermanence, and it can also establish [the thesis].
The absence of self is established by implication; this reason is certain, unlike the case of a jar or similar objects where the reason is subject to doubt.
The meaning of the text is as explained above. As for the phrase "because [it] exists":
This explanation clarifies the indeterminate [reason]. It is connected with the preceding passage on pleasure (*sukha*) to form a single continuous section.
That is to say, the point that "the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is observed to exist in things such as cloth, even when separated from a jar" refers to the aforementioned text:

because that [property] exists successively within the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). This means that since the reason—the property of being produced—exists in the cloth, which is a dissimilar instance where the jar is absent, it is therefore indeterminate.
"Certainty: it is not that the reason exists because of 'selflessness' and so forth apart from 'impermanence.
This means that if one uses 'the nature of being produced' as a collateral proof for selflessness, the reason is then certain; this explains the two characters 'not like' (非如) mentioned above.

Why? For example, if one were to establish that sound must be a jar, even if one were to concede this, the thesis would still be established [as a mere restatement], because of the nature of being produced."
It is just like the case of a jar. That reason [of being produced] also applies to things such as a non-jar or a cloth.
If sound is impermanent because it is produced, just as jars and so forth are impermanent, this reason does not apply specifically to the impermanence of those jars and so forth;
rather, this reason also applies to other instances of selflessness. For if jars and so forth are impermanent...

This is precisely selflessness (*anātman*). There is no selflessness existing separately outside of impermanence (*anitya*) that could serve as a distinct probans (*hetu*) for the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).
Therefore, if the probans of being produced establishes impermanence, it can simultaneously establish selflessness and so forth by implication; thus, this probans is definitive.
It is not like the probans of [being produced] in the case of a jar and the like, which results in uncertainty and other such fallacies.
What is meant by "functioning in a distinct location"?

An external opponent asks: because the property of the reason (hetu-dharma) in the thesis is distinct from the similar instances (sapakṣa), such as a jar, it is called a "distinct property" (*bhinna-dharma*).
Thus, jars, clothing, and so forth, are not called "distinct locations" relative to the locus of the property of the thesis. The intent of the current question is as follows:
For example, "being produced" is a property belonging to the proponent's thesis regarding sound. How could a property belonging to the proponent's thesis be established as existing in a jar?
[The opponent argues:
"Because it is similar to that [property in the subject], one does not state a different name for it."
This is the Master of the Treatise’s response. He states that the "produced nature" (kṛtakatva) residing in a jar and the "produced nature" residing in sound are extremely similar;

they are both collectively termed "produced nature. Since there is no evidence for a distinct name [for them], the cognition likewise functions with respect to jars and other things that belong to the same class.
This explains the phrase "certainly existing in the similar class" (sapakṣe sattvam eva).

Regarding the statement "it is identical," this means that the produced nature (*kṛtakatva*) in the pot is identical to the produced nature in the sound. Because they are extremely similar, it is said to be "identical.
It is like a thread passing through two flowers: one end of the thread passes through this flower, and the other end passes through that flower.

Flower. This is also like this. The nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is unitary, yet it resides upon two things: on the one hand, upon the sound "pot," and on the other hand, upon the pot itself.
Thus, there is no distinct entity that moves from one location to another and perishes. This is because it is a single [nature].
However, if analyzed in detail, the nature of being produced as it pertains to the sound and as it pertains to the pot are each distinct; they can only be described collectively as one.
The property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is what is called the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).
If it were not the property of the subject, the opponent would further object:
"If the property of being produced in a jar is not stated to be distinct from the property of being produced in sound," [then the reason would fail to be established].
How is it that this reason of being produced by effort (kṛtakatva-hetu) is called a property of the subject (pakṣadharma)?
It should also not be a property of the subject, because the reason of being produced by effort resides in the world and in jars.

Regarding the phrase "in this context, it is merely the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*)," this is the author of the treatise’s response. It means that within this property of the thesis, he states only that it is definitely a property of the thesis;

however, he does not intend to say that it is *exclusively* a property of the thesis. If one were to say it is the characteristic of a property of the thesis *only*, then this reason could not exist in relation to a jar.

[The opponent] says: "It is simply stated that [the property] is necessarily a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) with respect to the thesis (*pakṣa*); it is not said that the reason (*hetu*) is exclusively a property of the subject.
This is because there are reasons that are not properties of the subject, such as 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*), which exists equally on both a pot and the sky-flower."
If that is so [up to] "is called the thesis," the opponent further objects:
If the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) on a single pot in the world can also be called a reason (*hetu*), then...

Furthermore, that which is established as impermanent is also present in a single instance within the similar class (*sapakṣa*), such as a jar; it should therefore also be called the thesis (*pakṣa*).
If this were not so, then [the definition] would be equivalent to [the opponent's] objection.
The author of the treatise answers: Your objection, O outsider, that making the impermanence of a jar also constitute a thesis (pakṣa) is incorrect.
Why? Because what is to be established is stated in a distinct location. That is to say, sound, when compared to a jar, is a distinct location belonging to the jar;
it is in this distinct location that impermanence is established. As for the impermanence of the sound itself, it is [established] by the opponent.

It is not permitted to claim that this [impermanence] is non-existent; rather, it is now established by means of a reason (*hetu*). Thus, the impermanence residing in sound is stated as the probandum (*sādhya*).
This probandum may be termed the "thesis" (*pakṣa*). As for the impermanence residing in a jar, it is already established and commonly accepted by both the proponent and the opponent.

It need not be established. Since it is not intended to be established, how can it be called "that which is to be proven" (*sādhya*)? Since it is not that which is to be proven, it is not termed a "thesis" (*pakṣa*).
If the reason (*hetu*), such as the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), must be admitted by both the proponent and the opponent, then it is said that the reason must be without difference.
This is because a reason constitutes a reason only when it is mutually accepted by both parties. This is due to the mutual acceptance of the sound and the pot [as being produced].

Because both possess this reason, it only then constitutes an inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, it is not identical to the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established, for [the reason] is not commonly accepted as such;
the thesis is the thesis. Thus, they are not similar.
Furthermore, regarding these [terms] from "each one" up to "three kinds":

the preceding section provided a general explanation of the categories of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) in response to the inquiry concerning the nature of desire (*chanda*). From this point onward, there is an exegesis of the phrases "in the similar class" (*sapakṣa*) and so forth within the verse.
Regarding this very property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), there are three possibilities within the similar instances (*sapakṣa*): namely, its presence, its absence, and both.
Each of these three is further divided into three, thus resulting in nine types.

"Regarding that which exists up to that which does not exist" refers to the first of the three types [of logical reasons]. That is to say: it exists within the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and it exists within the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
"Either non-existent, or existent and non-existent; this is the first [type].

Regarding that which is non-existent in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), among the three types within the similar class, it is the second type, 'non-existent. Regarding the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), there are likewise three types, as previously described."
Regarding "and that which is concomitant":
within the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is the third type, the concomitant; within the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), there are likewise three types, as previously stated.
Each possesses these three kinds of distinctions.
This refers to the aforementioned three types each of "prior non-existence" and "simultaneous non-existence.
If one wishes [to establish] that there is no such thing as this "non-existence," the Vaiśeṣika school,
in response to the scriptural teachings, posits that sound is impermanent because it is a product (*kṛtakatva*), taking space (*ākāśa*) as...

Regarding the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*): since that scriptural teaching does not establish [the subject] as being situated in space, how can one say that this "produced nature" (*kṛtakatva*) is non-existent in that space?
This is the question posed by the opponent.
"Because [the reason] would fall into that same error (up to the point mentioned)" is the Master’s response.
This means: if that space were non-existent, then the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) would not apply to it;
this is established by scripture. If one were to argue as an opponent, one would certainly not maintain that the property of being produced applies to that non-existent space.

However, because the meaning of "exclusion" is established, it is called the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*). It is not necessary to point to a specific phenomenon that possesses the property of being a dissimilar instance for it to be so named.
Nevertheless, when debating with an opponent, one must have a dissimilar instance; the term refers to that which is remote [from the probandum]. Question:

If things such as rabbit horns are non-existent, and there is no counterpart to them, why would they not be considered dissimilar instances in the case of a thesis such as "sound is impermanent"? Answer: If...
