If one establishes a narrow thesis, stating that "sound is eternal," and establishes a broad reason, stating "because it is cognizable" (*prameyatvāt*), this reason is a "conclusive reason" (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*) in both the similar and dissimilar classes; it is exclusively [inconclusive] with respect to that narrow [thesis].
Thesis: With respect to both similar and dissimilar instances, that which is not contradictory to either is the nature of a doubtful reason (*saṃdigdhahetu*).

If one considers the broad thesis, "The internal self does not exist," then the reason "the nature of being an object of cognition" (*meyatva*) is a correct reason (*saddhetu*). Alternatively, regarding a narrow reason: [text continues].
Because it possesses the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), it is also the correct reason (*saddhetu*). It is subsumed under the category of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
Now, because one wishes to exclude a broad thesis (*pakṣa*), the word "only" (*mātra*) is used; furthermore, because one wishes to exclude a narrow reason, the word "only" is used.

That is to say, when this specific class of thesis is broad, the reason becomes inconclusive; it does not mean that there is doubt regarding the broad thesis. Moreover, when this broad reason is applied to a narrow thesis—
It brings about doubt; it is not due to that narrow reason itself. Regarding both that narrow thesis and the broad thesis, it becomes inconclusive.

Thus, with respect to broad and narrow theses, this common reason (sādhāraṇa-hetu) may be either conclusive or inconclusive. However, as for the uncommon reason (asādhāraṇa-hetu), it is invariably and always inconclusive, yet it is not [inconclusive] in the same sense [as the former]. Therefore, there is a distinction between them.
Regarding the phrase "if [it is] due to another distinction":
if the reason (*hetu*) established is present in both the similar and dissimilar instances within the category of the indeterminate (*anaikāntika*), it is not merely an indeterminate reason;
it is also a contradictory (*viruddha*) or a valid (*samyak*) reason. Regarding the phrase "because of the understanding of the distinction": by means of that which...
The establishment of the reason (*hetu*): because it does not occur within a portion of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is a definitive reason.

As the treatise establishes: "Sound is permanent" (the thesis); "because it lacks material obstruction" (the reason); "whatever lacks material obstruction is all likewise [permanent], such as space" (the similar example);
"if it were impermanent, it would possess material obstruction, such as a jar and so forth" (the dissimilar example). Here, space is taken as the similar class (*sapakṣa*).

Taking jars and the like as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), since these have already been excluded because they are impermanent and obstructive phenomena, one then takes space (*ākāśa*) as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
Therefore, this is a valid reason (*hetu*). However, if it were considered in relation to the mind, mental factors, and so forth, that reason would become contradictory (*viruddha*).

That is to say: "Sound is impermanent" (the thesis); "because it lacks substantial obstruction" (the reason); [if applied to mind, etc.,] all phenomena that lack substantial obstruction are entirely non-existent.
[The reason] "permanent" [is inconclusive], like the mind and mental factors (the similar example). If it were permanent, it would possess material resistance, like an atom (the dissimilar example).
These three [types of inconclusive reasons] are indeterminate when considered in relation to one part of the dissimilar class that is infinite, as they then become determinate;

however, when considered in relation to one part of the dissimilar class that is finite, they constitute doubt. As for the unique reason (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*), it does not exist at all within any [valid] thesis.
Because the meaning of emptiness differs, there is a distinction.
This is what is called "distinction";
it refers to the distinction between the four kinds of indeterminate [factors] and the unique [factors], as well as the distinction between the unique and the indeterminate.
If one were to claim that this is a valid reason for those who accept the eternal nature of sound, an opponent would object as follows:
"Since you say it is 'uncommon' (asādhāraṇa), how can you call it a 'perpetually indeterminate' reason?

If the reason is "the nature of being audible," then according to the Vaiśeṣikas, when establishing the category of "sameness-and-difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) regarding the nature of sound, its essence is [admitted by them to be] an object of cognition. However, [this reason] is...
That which is constant ought to be a valid reason (*saddhetu*). Why, then, is it said to be "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*)?
If, at that time (and so forth), it were a cause for doubt (*saṃśayahetu*), this would be a general objection.
If the Vaiśeṣika, at the time of establishing his thesis, is dull-witted and lacks wisdom, he will be unable to [provide a response].
Regarding that proponent of the theory of sound (*śabdavādin*), who presents "being produced" or "being originated by volitional effort without interval" as the reason for impermanence:

while it may be possible to counter him with the fallacy of "contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) against that Vaiśeṣika, such a contradictory certainty is necessarily obtainable when the Vaiśeṣika establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) against the proponent of sound. Therefore...
The reason based on what is heard is indeterminate. To say they are "simultaneous" means they are established at the same time. Question:

While the nature of what is heard may be determinate, it is said that [the reason] universally encompasses that which is always indeterminate. Although the other four distinct meanings possess determinacy, they too should be considered always indeterminate in terms of their specific meanings.
Answer: Because the other four meanings are always present, they are not merely indeterminate and uncommon; rather—
Regarding Vātsyāyana, it is therefore said that [the reason] is exclusively non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*). The following explains how these two constitute a cause for doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*):
first, regarding the meaning of the term "property-possessor" (*dharmin*), whether it be eternal or non-eternal, they are mutually contradictory and cannot coexist; thus, both are grounds for doubt.

Regarding this established thesis, although permanence and impermanence cannot be definitively fixed, if one were to debate their relative merit, the former would be defeated and the latter victorious,
like a game of "slow-to-kill" chess.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that one should seek certainty by relying on this [system] because the power of its manifest teaching is superior:
the assessment of the relative strength of the arguments of Master Dignāga is as previously described.

According to reason, as to what is incorrect and what is correct, that which is established by Vaiśeṣika as impermanent is correct, because the power of its manifest teaching is superior. That is to say, first, the power of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [The world...]

It is directly perceived that sound is intermittent, as there are times when it is not heard. Between these two—direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference based on scripture (*āgama-anumāna*)—the latter is superior because it possesses the force of inferential scripture.
Since the theory of sound (*śabda-śāstra*) relies solely on inferential scripture, it is inferior. Furthermore, this was spoken by the Buddha.
It is also said that sound is impermanent. Because the Buddha is supreme among all teachers, he is "Vaiśeṣika" (the Supreme One).

Therefore, based on these two excellences—his manifest teaching and his supremacy—one should seek the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through reflection, regardless of whether they precede or follow one another.

Even if the Vaiśeṣikas were to establish their position first, because the Buddha’s manifest teaching is superior, their reasoning would still be correct. Furthermore, it is explained that the Tathāgata perceives directly that sound is impermanent.

The teachings he constantly proclaims should be regarded as the Buddha’s own teachings; therefore, the Buddha’s teachings are supreme. One may rely upon this supreme teaching to contemplate and seek the impermanence of sound.

Furthermore, "teaching" refers to the ultimate teaching (*āptāgama*), which means that among all the verbal teachings existing in the world, those that accord with reason constitute the ultimate teaching. It is directly perceived in the world that sound arises from conditions, just as...

Just as with a jar or a basin, whose substance is produced and which does not exist when not being heard, one perceives this through direct observation in order to give rise to the authoritative teaching on impermanence;
since the Vaiśeṣika school holds the same view, it is established that sound is impermanent.

Regarding the phrase "summarizing the preceding verses" (*shè shàng sòng*), it means summarizing the prose that precedes them. Although the subsequent verses clarify other threefold contradictions not present in the preceding text,
there is no fault, because [the term] does not state that it summarizes *only* the preceding verses.
If a phenomenon is "unshared" (as far as "all are the nature of the *hetu*"), this verse refers to the six types of "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reasons.
"Phenomenon" refers to the reason-phenomenon. "Unshared" refers to the reason of being the nature of what is heard (*śruta*).

"Shared" refers to the four reasons such as the nature of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), and so forth. Because these are common to both the similar and dissimilar classes (*sapakṣa* and *vipakṣa*), they are not determinative.
Regarding "contradiction": this refers to the "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*) established by the Grammarians (*Śābdika*) and the Vaiśeṣikas.
Regarding "pervading all": these six types of indeterminate reasons pervade all phenomena throughout the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding "all of which are of the nature of a cause for doubt": with respect to all those phenomena, these six factors constitute doubt or an indeterminate reason.
"If one were to falsely prove that a phenomenon exists (and so forth), provided there is no contradiction or sublation, this verse presents a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*).
If the preceding reason-phenomenon is able to falsely and erroneously prove the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of a phenomenon..."
There are cases where there is a contradiction regarding the specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) of the subject (*dharmin*), yet this does not constitute a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).

This is because it is among the five faults of the thesis, or rather, it is a contradictory reason (*viruddhahetu*) and not a fault of the thesis itself. According to the preceding discussion on the distributed [reason], there is only the single contradictory reason concerning the specific nature of the subject.
Regarding the "examination of the thesis-attribute" (pakṣadharma) [up to] the "pseudo-reason" (hetvābhāsa):
this summarizes the indeterminate (anaikāntika) and contradictory (viruddha) fallacies.

When an opponent examines the reason-attribute of the proponent, if they consider it to be a valid reason, yet upon engaging in critical investigation and deliberation, their mind becomes doubtful and indeterminate, resulting in hesitation. This constitutes the sixth [fallacy].
Regarding the cause of certainty (*niścaya-hetu*): it is called "examination" (*parīkṣā*) because it is not certain; thus, one examines it.
If one observes the reason (*hetu*) and property (*dharma*) of the proponent and finds them to contradict the properties (*dharmin*, etc. desired by that opponent, then a perversion occurs.

Apart from these four contradictory reasons (*viruddha-hetu*), as well as the two fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) consisting of the uncertain (*anaikāntika*) and the contradictory (*viruddha*), there are no other names for fallacious reasons. This is because...
The ancient masters of Hetuvidyā (Logic), or the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others, do not designate the "nature-as-cause" (*svabhāvahetu*) as "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*);

rather, they assign it a different name. They likewise assign a distinct name to the "contradictory" (*viruddha*). To refute these divergent views, it is said that "apart from these, there are no fallacious reasons.

Regarding the four types of unestablished reasons (*asiddha*), they are fundamentally not properties of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*); however, they are now classified as "fallacious" (*ābhāsa*) in relation to the property of the thesis. Thus, [they are not considered separate categories].

This is called a "semblance-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*). Furthermore, another interpretation is that here, in view of the two classes—the similar (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar (*vipakṣa*)—one clarifies what is authentic and what is a semblance, rather than discussing [the reason] as being unestablished (*asiddha*).
Having thus distinguished the reason and the semblance-reason, the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) shall now be explained.

This concludes the transition from the higher realm to birth in the lower realm. According to the Sanskrit original, it says *darśanānta-hetu*. This is correctly interpreted as establishing the cause based on the extreme of views (*dṛṣṭi-anta*).

However, while the meaning that "the reason is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) is clearly manifest, the two characteristics—that it exists in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and does not exist in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)—are not explicitly shown.

This prevents the understanding of the thesis (*pakṣa*) from reaching its ultimate conclusion. Now, these two characteristics—the presence in similar instances and the absence in dissimilar instances—are further elucidated through an analogy.
It causes one to understand the views of the various schools; when these reach their ultimate excess, they are called "extremes of view" (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For now, following the traditional translation, we shall call them "metaphors" (*dṛṣṭānta*), which means "to explain through illustration."
Regarding the statement "the reason is similar [to the example]":

this means that the reason stated is followed by the thesis (*pakṣa*). This is precisely the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). First, its reason is stated; the thesis then follows accordingly.

It is said that whatever is produced by causes is impermanent. When the nature of being produced is known in a certain locus, its impermanence is necessarily known to follow it, just as when a mother cow is present, her calf must necessarily follow.
Thus, when the nature of being produced reaches objects such as a jar, its impermanence also necessarily follows and reaches objects such as jars and basins. Therefore...
The reason for its being a product is established as residing in the sound; likewise, its impermanence also comes to reside in that sound.
Since impermanence in a jar is commonly accepted, it is real; it is not called a "thesis" (pakṣa) merely because it resembles a thesis.

That "the thesis does not exist without a reason" refers to the dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta). First the absence of the thesis is stated, and then the absence of the reason is stated, as in the following statement:
That which is eternally abiding is not something produced; it merely lacks any locus for the establishment of a thesis, such as space and so forth.
This cause of being produced necessarily does not exist therein, just as where a mother cow does not go, her calf does not go.
In this case, there is no locus for the thesis of impermanence, being void like space and so forth; thus, the cause of being produced necessarily [does not apply].
Since it is certain that [sound] does not exist [as permanent], one knows that sound has a cause for its production and is therefore certainly impermanent.

These two are called "illustrative examples" (*dṛṣṭānta*). All others are similar to these; that is, apart from these two primary illustrations, all are merely similar illustrations corresponding to these primary ones.
The "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) refers here to the statement of the reason (*hetu*):
namely, that sound is impermanent because it is produced by volitional effort (*prayatnānantarīyaka*).
This cites the thesis and the reason. This merely briefly cites the "nature-as-reason" (*svabhāva-hetu*) among those [three types of reasons] he has formulated; other cases are the same as this.
For instance, that which is produced by diligent effort and uninterrupted application is all impermanent.
This refers to the illustrative essence (*dṛṣṭānta-svabhāva*).

"The jar and so forth" refers to the actual entities upon which the illustration is based. When taking the illustrative essence itself, it is simply that which is produced; this is conjoined with impermanence to form the illustration.
The character "者" (zhě) carries the sense of inclusion. Because this reason serves as an analogy, it constitutes one of the three characteristics of a valid reason (*trairūpya*).
Since there is no other distinct phenomenon [to serve as the example], only that which is produced (*kṛtaka*) serves as the primary analogy.

However, because the body of the analogy can demonstrate impermanence, it also includes that which is most impermanent as an analogy. Why, then, does the reason not likewise include that which is most impermanent? Answer:
Because of the statement "due to being produced," this very statement simultaneously encompasses the supreme thesis.
That is to say, because it is "produced," within the statement "it is impermanent," the ambiguity is eliminated; thus, the statement is conjoined with the supreme thesis of impermanence.
However, because the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) appear distinct, the thesis is stated separately from the reason.

Although both the reason and the thesis are present within the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is intended to show that the "produced nature" (*kṛtakatva*) is common to both in order to clarify the meaning of impermanence (*anityatva*); therefore, it is included within the example and is not called the thesis.
As for other passages in the text where the impermanence of a jar is stated as the thesis, this is merely a provisional designation based on the category of the thesis itself.
This is called the thesis (*pakṣa*). Regarding its dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), it is likewise fundamentally without a reason (*hetu*) and, moreover, lacks a thesis;
this is explained in the same manner as the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). As for the "dissimilar" (*vaidharmya*):
This is the citation of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
That is to say, those who hold the view that all things are eternal are not produced through uninterrupted effort;
this is the illustrative subject (*dharmin*).
"Such as space, etc. refers to the objective basis for the illustration. "Etc. includes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

In the Mahāyāna, it includes all seven unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). If it contradicts worldly convention, etc., then whatever is commonly accepted is included in "etc. and "all-inclusive."
"The former is a negation (*paryudāsa*), while the latter merely stops confusion" distinguishes the difference between the two examples.
The former is the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); the latter is the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). All phenomena possess two characteristics:
first, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is apprehended only by the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, and not by the scattered mental consciousness or others.

The second is the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). This refers to the mental consciousness and so forth in a distracted state of mind. Names and words express only the universal characteristic;
they cannot express the causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is beyond verbal expression.

To express the universal characteristic, one must first negate and exclude other phenomena before this phenomenon can be expressed and revealed. For example, the word "blue" excludes what is not blue, such as yellow and so forth, and only then can it reveal that [specific color].
Regarding the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of blue: if it did not exclude yellow and so forth, then when one says "blue" or "yellow," those [other colors] would necessarily follow.
All linguistic expressions (nāma-vyavahāra) that intend to designate a given phenomenon must exclude other designations; there is no designation of a phenomenon that does not involve exclusion.

However, there are linguistic expressions that merely exclude other phenomena without further designating anything else, such as saying "there is no blue," which does not further manifest anything distinct.
There is no essence of blue [in the term]. Now, regarding the concordant example (*dṛṣṭānta*):
"All things produced by immediate effort" excludes what is not produced by immediate effort and reveals what is produced by immediate effort;

all such things are impermanent, excluding what is permanent, and thus they express and reveal phenomena that arise and perish. Therefore, it is said that the former is exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and the latter is affirmation (*vidhi*).
Regarding the analogy for this distinct dharma: those things that are "permanent" (nitya) merely negate impermanence; thus they are called "permanent.

One does not intend to provide a further, separate definition of permanence. That is to say, it is simply "unproduced" (akṛtaka), merely negating what is produced, rather than separately defining or manifesting the essential nature of the unproduced dharma.
This meaning is simply that wherever the thesis of impermanence is absent, there is no production whatsoever. It is only...
This merely stops over-extension; it does not intend to define or reveal the essential nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Therefore, it is said that the latter [definition] only stops over-extension.
This is because the meaning is inferred through conjunction and disjunction.

This explains the aforementioned distinction. Because one infers by means of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) to conjoin with the reason (*hetu*) of the original thesis (*pakṣa*), it is a negation that achieves expression.
Since the reason of the original thesis is itself a negative expression (*paryudāsa*), one merely uses a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) to exclude the reason of the original thesis;
thus, it serves only to prevent confusion and does not intend to express anything else separately.
"Even though one dwells [in the world]... until the establishment of the meaning":
this indicates that for every thesis established, there exists a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) in relation to every position.

Because of the understanding of the intent of the dissimilar example as explained above, even in relation to the scriptures and so forth, the existence of that nature of great empty space (*mahākāśatva*) is not admitted.

Furthermore, it is by taking space (*ākāśa*) as a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) that this [point] can be made manifest. However, even in the absence of a formal thesis (*pakṣa*), the meaning of being causeless—such as in the case of a single hair or the like—is established as a dissimilar example;
it is not necessary for a dissimilar example to possess an actual substantial entity (*dravyasat*). Thus, it serves as a dissimilar example.
Even if there were something to be expressed [by the reason], this would not be problematic.
Furthermore, regarding the question "By what cause (up to) is the thesis not present?", this explains the human perspective:
for what reason do you, the proponent of the treatise, state the "reason reaching the subject" (*pūrvavat-hetu*) first in the primary positive example (*sapakṣa*)?
In the subsequent statement of the negative example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the absence of the thesis (*pakṣābhāva*) is stated first, followed by the absence of the reason (*hetvabhāva*).

This differs from the positive example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), where the absence of the reason is stated first and the absence of the thesis follows. By the logic of the negative example, since the absence of the thesis has already been stated first, [the absence of the reason must follow].
Since it is stated later that the reason (*hetu*) is absent, why is the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) not stated first, followed by the thesis (*pakṣa*) and then the reason?
[This is] because it is stated in this manner (and so forth), and not stated in a distorted way.

Below this, [the author] first presents the prose version of the elder brother. By means of these two metaphors, because they are stated differently from what was previously established, one is able to demonstrate the reason (*hetu*) of "exertion" (*prayatna*):
that it is necessarily present in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and entirely absent in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
Thus, it is not a mistaken statement. For example, if within the similar instances one says: "Sound is impermanent" (the thesis), "because it is produced by exertion" (the reason). If...
To state that "all things which are impermanent have exertion as their cause" is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the similar class (*sapakṣa*),
because lightning belongs to the category of the impermanent, yet it lacks the cause of exertion. Furthermore,

if one were to claim that "whatever is not produced by exertion is permanent," this would be incorrect, for although lightning and the like are not produced by exertion, they are nonetheless not permanent.
Therefore, one cannot say that what is not produced by effort is eternal.
Furthermore, it is said in verse: “[... as for conjunction, separation, etc. This is the response provided by citing the verse.
The phrase “conjunction, separation, etc. refers back to the objection. “Conjunction” refers to the concordant example (*sapakṣa*); “separation” [refers to the discordant example (*vipakṣa*)].

This refers to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). "Etc. (*ādi*) means "and so forth. If you, the opponent, say that this conjunction (*sādharmya*) indicates the exclusion (*vyatireka) [of the reason] from the thesis first and then the reason, whereas the exclusion indicates the conjunction first and then the reason;

[we reply that] the first two phrases of the text answer the pervasive reason (*vyāpaka-hetu*), while the subsequent four characters and the word "and" (*ca*) answer the non-pervasive reason (*avyāpaka-hetu*) produced by immediate effort (*prayatnānantarīyaka*). If [you argue] with...
Regarding the separation of the illustration from the reason and the placement of the reason before the thesis:
one should then prove its permanence by means of the reason "the nature of being non-produced," because it is said that "all things that are not produced are permanent.

If this were the case, then what you originally asserted as the thesis—impermanence—would be established as its opposite; thus, the thesis itself would independently establish permanence as its own thesis. Therefore, it is said:

It would follow that it is not what was intended to be stated. Furthermore, since emptiness is permanent, and this is accepted by both the proponent and the opponent, why is it necessary to establish it?
If it were to be established, it would follow that it is not what was intended to be stated, because one must state the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Since it is impossible to establish "impermanence" as the thesis while separately establishing the meaning of "permanence," one should not first state the reason (*hetu*) of "not being produced. Subsequently...

It is taught that permanence is taken as the thesis (*pakṣa*). If one were to separate the application (*upanaya*) from the thesis and place the reason (*hetu*) before it, then one would have to take impermanence as the reason to prove what is produced. This is because it would be stated: "All impermanent phenomena are produced."
If this were the case, then your fundamental thesis of impermanence would not be established;
instead, a separate thesis—that "that which is produced" is impermanent—would be established. Therefore it is said: "If that were so, it would result in something other than what was stated.

Furthermore, since the pot's being produced is admitted by both the proponent and the opponent, what remains to be established? If there were anything to be established, it would likewise result in something other than what was stated.

This is because it is the very thesis (*pakṣa*). It would follow that [the thesis] is not what is being stated. Question: If it is universally accepted that a jar is a product (*kṛtaka*), it need not be established further.
Likewise, since the impermanence of a jar is equally believed by both parties, it too should not need to be established.

If one were to say, "All products are impermanent," and then use sound as a product to prove its impermanence, one could not establish impermanence; for the jar itself, which is already established as a product, is simply impermanent.
[This is] a fault. If one establishes "the produced" (*kṛtaka*) by means of "impermanence" (*anitya*), it does not assist in proving that "the produced" is impermanent in relation to sound;

rather, it establishes "the produced" independently. Since "the produced" is thus established [independently], one cannot establish "impermanence" as the thesis (*pakṣa*), because it would then be establishing "the produced" separately.
Therefore, one should not first state "impermanence" and subsequently state "the produced. Question: Regarding the application (*upanaya*) to the concordant example (*sapakṣa*) and the thesis...

Regarding the reason (*hetu*): it should follow the order of stating the thesis (*pakṣa*) first and the reason later. In this case, the principle of "awareness" (*buddhi*) is superior to that of "the person" (*puruṣa*), which is held [by the opponent].

If one says that [the reason] is not "pervasive" (*avyāpin*) and thus not the thesis, this merely reverses the original reason of being "produced immediately following volitional effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*).

To say it is not pervasive means that the reason of "being produced by volitional effort" is broad, while the thesis of "eternality" is narrow; therefore, because this thesis does not pervade the reason, it is said to be non-pervasive. Furthermore, there is no...

The reason for "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) is that it is always broad, whereas the reason for "produced by effort" (*prayatnaja*) is narrow; because the reason does not encompass the entire subject, it is called "non-pervasive.

If one were to conjoin the dissimilar class with the preceding reason and the subsequent thesis, then one would have to prove its permanence by means of [the property of] "not being produced immediately following effort."
If one were to apply the analogy by placing the thesis first and the reason last, then one would have to establish "impermanence" as being "produced by effort and exertion.
If this were the case, it would result in proving what has not been stated. This refutation follows the previous explanation.
Such a fault does not pervade the reason of being "produced by effort," which is identical to the reason of being "a product" (*kṛtaka*). Thus, the present text should [be understood accordingly].

Regarding the term "not-pervasive" (*avyāpin*): it is stated as "not-pervasive" only by way of abbreviation; it does not indicate that this reason of non-pervasiveness separately establishes the thesis that "non-self" (*anātman*) is pervasive.
